0.title: The Throne of Grace: The Book of 2 Samuel
0.overview:
Second Samuel is the story of a king — but it is more profoundly the story of a covenant. At its center stands the most important promise in the entire Old Testament: I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever (7:13). The Davidic covenant is the theological spine of 2 Samuel, and everything before it (David's painful, glorious consolidation of the kingdom) and everything after it (the catastrophic sins, the rebellions, the griefs of his later years) must be read in its light. God's covenant with David is unconditional, permanent, and eschatological — it will not be broken by David's failures or by his successors' failures, because it rests on the character of God, not the character of David.

The book divides naturally into three movements. The first (chapters 1–10) traces the arc of David's rise: the lament for Saul and Jonathan, the seven-year civil war, the coronation as king of all Israel, the conquest of Jerusalem, the tumultuous bringing of the ark to the city of David, and the great covenant of chapter 7. These are the years of unambiguous triumph, and even here the narrative is honest: the ark kills Uzzah; Michal's contempt ends her marriage; David's wars, however just, are also costly. But the dominant note is grace — the shepherd boy from Bethlehem, anointed in the sight of his brothers, now sits on the throne of a united Israel and receives the most extraordinary promise ever spoken to a human being.

The second movement (chapters 11–20) is the great unraveling. David sees Bathsheba, takes her, commits adultery, arranges Uriah's murder, and lives in self-deception for perhaps a year until Nathan arrives with a parable and a verdict: You are the man. His repentance — recorded in Psalm 51 — is the deepest and most honest in the OT, and it stands in permanent contrast to Saul's self-justification. But the consequences are real and devastating: the child dies, Amnon rapes Tamar, Absalom murders Amnon and launches a coup, and David flees Jerusalem weeping, barefoot, ascending the Mount of Olives — one of the most heartbreaking scenes in all of Scripture, and one of the most Christ-haunted.

The third movement (chapters 21–24) is a kind of appendix: poems, lists, and a final plague that ends at the threshing floor of Araunah — the very site where Solomon will build the temple, where Abraham offered Isaac, where the intersection of divine judgment and divine mercy is most concentrated in all of human history. The book ends not with David's triumph but with his sacrifice, and with the mercy that stops the destroying angel above Jerusalem. It is, in miniature, the grammar of the entire gospel.

Christologically, 2 Samuel is inexhaustible. The Davidic covenant of chapter 7 is the direct seedbed of the NT's proclamation that Jesus is the Son of David (Matt. 1:1; Luke 1:32–33; Rom. 1:3; Rev. 22:16). Mephibosheth's story (chapter 9) is one of the OT's most perfect pictures of grace — the crippled heir of a dead dynasty, brought to the king's table, not because of what he was but because of the covenant David made with his father Jonathan. David's lament over Absalom — O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you (18:33) — is the cry of a father for a son who died in rebellion, and it reaches across the centuries to the Father who gave his Son for those who were at war with him. And the final threshing-floor sacrifice, where David insists on paying for what he offers — I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing (24:24) — is the eternal principle of substitutionary sacrifice: the offering must cost the one who offers it.

1.title: The Lament of the Bow
1.text: <sup>1</sup>After the death of Saul, when David had returned from striking down the Amalekites, David remained two days in Ziklag.<sup>2</sup>And on the third day, behold, a man came from Saul's camp, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. And when he came to David, he fell to the ground and paid homage.<sup>3</sup>David said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel."<sup>4</sup>And David said to him, "How did it go? Tell me." And I took the crown that was on his head and the armlet that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord."<sup>11</sup>Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men who were with him.<sup>12</sup>And they mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for the people of the LORD and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.<sup>13</sup>And David said to the young man who told him, "Where do you come from?" He said:<sup>19</sup>"Your glory, O Israel, is slain on your high places! How the mighty have fallen!<sup>20</sup>Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.<sup>21</sup>"You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew or rain upon you, nor fields of offerings! "Jonathan lies slain on your high places.<sup>26</sup>I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women.<sup>27</sup>"How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war perished!"
1.overview:
The book opens forty miles from where the last one ended, in a burnt town, with a man who does not yet know. On the third day a messenger arrives with torn clothes and earth on his head — which is the recognised sign of a disaster and, in this case, also a costume. His account is detailed, and it is false: he says he found Saul leaning on his spear and killed him at his own request, but the previous chapter watched Saul fall on his own sword while his armour-bearer looked on. He is a scavenger who found the body, took the crown and the armlet, and spent three days walking south working out what to say. He assumed the hunted man would be pleased. He read David completely wrong.

And he is an Amalekite — the nation Saul lost the kingdom for sparing, and the nation David has spent the last three days cutting down at Ziklag. The narrator sets the word down and says nothing.

David tears his clothes and gives the whole day to grief before he passes any sentence: for Saul, for Jonathan, for the people of the LORD, for the house of Israel. Then the question that every reader of 1 Samuel has heard twice already — how is it you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed? He held that principle for years when it cost him everything, and he enforces it on his first day with power, when keeping it costs nothing.

Then the Song of the Bow, written down and ordered taught to Judah — a poem honouring the man whose crown he is about to wear, composed by the one person in Israel with the most material for a different poem. It curses the mountain, mourns a shield nobody will oil again, tells the daughters of Israel to remember the scarlet and the gold, and ends alone with Jonathan. And two things are missing from it: any word about David, and any mention of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — A Man Came from Saul's Camp
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the third day after Ziklag a man arrives with his clothes torn and earth on his head, and falls to the ground (vv. 1-2). The army has fled, many are dead, and Saul and his son Jonathan are also dead (vv. 3-4). David asks how he knows, and gets a detailed story: he came by chance on Mount Gilboa, found Saul leaning on his spear with the chariots closing in, and killed him at his own request — because I was sure that he could not live after he had fallen (vv. 5-10). And he produces the crown and the armlet.
verseByVerse.theology: The story is false, and the reader knows it because the previous chapter was watched at close range: Saul fell on his own sword, and his armour-bearer saw that Saul was dead before falling on his own (1 Sam. 31:4-5). This man is a scavenger who came across the body, stripped the royal insignia off it, and invented a part for himself.
verseByVerse.examples: And he is an Amalekite. Saul lost the kingdom for sparing that nation (1 Sam. 15), and David has come to Ziklag straight from cutting down the Amalekites who burned it (1 Sam. 30). The narrator sets the word down and offers no comment whatever.

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Saul, when David had returned from striking down the Amalekites, David remained two days in Ziklag. And on the third day, behold, a man came from Saul's camp, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. And when he came to David, he fell to the ground and paid homage. David said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel." And David said to him, "How did it go? Tell me." And he answered, "The people fled from the battle, and also many of the people have fallen and are dead, and Saul and his son Jonathan are also dead." Then David said to the young man who told him, "How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?" And the young man who told him said, "By chance I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul leaning on his spear, and behold, the chariots and the horsemen were close upon him. And when he looked behind him, he saw me, and called to me. And I answered, 'Here I am.' And he said to me, 'Who are you?' I answered him, 'I am an Amalekite.' And he said to me, 'Stand beside me and kill me, for anguish has seized me, and yet my life still lingers.' So I stood beside him and killed him, because I was sure that he could not live after he had fallen. And I took the crown that was on his head and the armlet that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After the death of Saul, when David had returned from striking down the Amalekites, David remained two days in Ziklag.'

Two books meet in that sentence.

1 Samuel ended on Mount Gilboa with a body on a wall and the men of Jabesh-gilead walking all night to take it down. This one opens forty miles south, in a burnt town, with a man who does not yet know any of it.

Note where he has just been: striking down the Amalekites. Hold that for nine verses.

'And on the third day, behold, a man came from Saul's camp, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. And when he came to David, he fell to the ground and paid homage.'

Torn clothes and earth on the head are the recognised signs of a man carrying a disaster, and they are also, in this case, a costume.

He falls on his face — which is what you do before a king, not before a mercenary captain in a burnt village, and the gesture tells you what he thinks he is doing.

'David said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel."'

'And David said to him, "How did it go? Tell me."'

Three words, and everything hangs on them.

'And he answered, "The people fled from the battle, and also many of the people have fallen and are dead, and Saul and his son Jonathan are also dead."'

He puts it in the right order, worst last, and the last four words are the ones that matter to the man he is speaking to.

'Then David said to the young man who told him, "How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?"'

The right question, and it is a lawyer's question. How do you know?

'And the young man who told him said, "By chance I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul leaning on his spear, and behold, the chariots and the horsemen were close upon him."'

By chance I happened to be on Mount Gilboa.

Nobody happens to be on a battlefield by chance. Men are on a battlefield after the fighting for one reason, and it is to go through the pockets of the dead.

'"And when he looked behind him, he saw me, and called to me. And I answered, 'Here I am.' And he said to me, 'Who are you?' I answered him, 'I am an Amalekite.' And he said to me, 'Stand beside me and kill me, for anguish has seized me, and yet my life still lingers.'"'

'"So I stood beside him and killed him, because I was sure that he could not live after he had fallen. And I took the crown that was on his head and the armlet that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord."'

It is a good story, told with detail, and it is not true.

The reader knows this because the reader was standing there. The previous chapter reports Saul's death at close range and from a witness: the archers found him, he asked his armour-bearer to finish him, the man refused out of fear, so Saul took his own sword and fell upon it. And when his armour-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died with him (1 Sam. 31:4-5).

There was no Amalekite in that account, and there was no breath left in Saul to negotiate with.

So what happened is this. A scavenger came over the ridge after the fighting, found the king's body among the dead, took the crown off the head and the armlet off the arm, and walked south for three days working out what to say. He has calculated exactly what he thinks a rival claimant would pay for: not the news, which anyone could bring, but the deed. He wants to be the man who did it.

Everything about the invention tells you how he read David. He assumed that the fugitive would be pleased. He assumed that the years of being hunted had produced what they usually produce. He assumed that a crown and a corpse were a business opportunity.

He was wrong about all of it, and it kills him.

Then there is the word he uses to identify himself, and the writer leaves it entirely alone.

I am an Amalekite.

Saul lost the kingdom over Amalek. That was the command he would not carry out at Gilgal, and the reason Samuel gave him at Endor for everything that happened the next day (1 Sam. 15:1-23; 28:18). David has spent the last three days killing Amalekites who burned this very town, and four hundred of them got away on camels.

And here is one, standing in front of him, holding Saul's crown, claiming to have finished the man who spared his people.

The narrator sets it down and says nothing at all about it, which is his manner. He has done the same thing all through the last book. He puts the facts next to each other and lets whoever is reading carefully do the rest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — Your Own Mouth Has Testified Against You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David and all his men tear their clothes, and mourn and weep and fast until evening — for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for the people of the LORD and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword (vv. 11-12). Then he turns to the messenger: how is it you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed? (v. 14). He has him struck down, with the verdict: your blood be on your head, for your own mouth has testified against you, saying, "I have killed the LORD's anointed" (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The order of the day matters. Hours of public grief come first, and the sentence afterwards. Nothing here is a calculated performance, and the list he mourns for runs outward: Saul, Jonathan, the people of the LORD, the house of Israel.
verseByVerse.examples: He is condemned on his testimony, not his deed — and he almost certainly did not do it. That is the point of your own mouth. And the principle enforced is the one David held through seven chapters of being hunted, at a cost his own men could not understand: nobody puts a hand on the LORD's anointed. He applies it on his first day with power exactly as he applied it with none.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men who were with him. And they mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for the people of the LORD and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword. And David said to the young man who told him, "Where do you come from?" And he answered, "I am the son of a sojourner, an Amalekite." David said to him, "How is it you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed?" Then David called one of the young men and said, "Go, execute him." And he struck him down so that he died. And David said to him, "Your blood be on your head, for your own mouth has testified against you, saying, 'I have killed the LORD's anointed.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men who were with him.'

Before he says a word he tears his clothes, and six hundred men tear theirs.

'And they mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for the people of the LORD and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.'

The whole day goes to grief, and the list runs outward from the personal to the national.

For Saul — first, and the man had hunted him for the better part of a decade. For Jonathan his son — and there is a whole life in that clause, which will get its own verses at the end of the chapter. For the people of the LORD, and for the house of Israel — the army is gone and the northern towns have been abandoned to the Philistines.

It should be said that this is not a performance, because a reader is entitled to wonder. There is no audience here but his own men, who know exactly what Saul did to him. He is not building a reputation with a room full of Judahites; he is in a burnt village with the people who ran with him, and every one of them buried something at Ziklag a week ago.

He also does the grieving before he does the judging, and that order matters. The Amalekite is standing there the whole time.

'And David said to the young man who told him, "Where do you come from?" And he answered, "I am the son of a sojourner, an Amalekite."'

The question is put a second time, and this time the answer is fuller: the son of a sojourner — a resident foreigner, someone living under Israel's law without being of Israel.

That detail matters to what follows. A ger living in Israel was bound by the same law as the native-born and protected by it (Lev. 24:22). He is not a foreign combatant. By his own account he is a man who lived under that law and put his hand on the king.

'David said to him, "How is it you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed?"'

There is the sentence, and anybody who has read 1 Samuel has heard it before.

It is what David said in the cave at Engedi when his men had Saul at their mercy: the LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed, to put out my hand against him (1 Sam. 24:6). It is what he said to Abishai standing over the sleeping king in the camp at Hachilah: who can put out his hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless? (1 Sam. 26:9).

He held that principle for years when holding it cost him everything — when he was hunted, hungry, living in caves, and had two clear opportunities to end it in an afternoon. His own men argued with him about it twice.

Now he has the crown in front of him and no one to answer to, and he enforces the same rule from the other side of it.

That is the test that matters. Almost anyone can hold a principle while it is costing them, and feel righteous doing it. The question is whether it survives the day the power arrives, when keeping it costs nothing and nobody would notice its absence.

'Then David called one of the young men and said, "Go, execute him." And he struck him down so that he died.'

It is done immediately and it is done by somebody else, and both of those are deliberate.

'And David said to him, "Your blood be on your head, for your own mouth has testified against you, saying, 'I have killed the LORD's anointed.'"'

Your own mouth has testified against you.

Read that carefully, because it tells you David knows.

He does not say you killed the king. He says you said you killed the king. The sentence is passed on the confession, not on the act — and the act, in all likelihood, never happened.

Whether David has worked out the whole lie is not stated. What is certain is that he has been handed a self-declared regicide, in his own words, unprompted, in front of witnesses, and he treats the man exactly as the man has described himself.

There is a hard justice in it that Scripture does not soften. He came looking to be paid for claiming to have done a thing, and he was paid for it. A man who will invent a murder to advance himself has told you what he is, and David took him at his word.

It is also, in a way the man could never have anticipated, the fairest possible reading of him. He was offered the account of himself he had chosen to give.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Tell It Not in Gath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David composes a lament and orders it taught to the people of Judah — the Song of the Bow, recorded in the Book of Jashar (vv. 17-18). Your glory, O Israel, is slain on your high places! How the mighty have fallen! (v. 19). Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon (v. 20). He curses the mountain: let there be no dew or rain upon you, where the shield of Saul, not anointed with oil, was defiled (v. 21). Their courage is praised without reservation (vv. 22-23), and the women are called to weep for the king who clothed you luxuriously in scarlet (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: A shield's leather was rubbed with oil to keep it supple and turn a blade. Saul's lies on Gilboa unattended, and the picture is of a king's gear left to rot in the rain — which is why the next line asks the rain not to come.
verseByVerse.examples: Stop at verse 24. David remembers Saul's reign for what it actually gave the nation: prosperity, scarlet, gold on the clothing. Whatever else he had grounds to say, he says the true good thing, and he says it to the women who once sang the song that nearly got him killed.

verseByVerse.quote: And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and Jonathan his son, and he said it should be taught to the people of Judah; behold, it is written in the Book of Jashar. He said: "Your glory, O Israel, is slain on your high places! How the mighty have fallen! Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult. "You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew or rain upon you, nor fields of offerings! For there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, not anointed with oil. "From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan turned not back, and the sword of Saul returned not empty. "Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely! In life and in death they were not divided; they were swifter than eagles; they were stronger than lions. "You daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you luxuriously in scarlet, who put ornaments of gold on your apparel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and Jonathan his son, and he said it should be taught to the people of Judah; behold, it is written in the Book of Jashar.'

He does not just grieve. He writes it down and puts it on the syllabus.

The lament is given a title — the Song of the Bow — and an instruction: teach it to the people of Judah. This is grief turned into something a nation can learn and repeat, so that what a whole generation feels about Saul's death will be shaped by what David felt about it.

Consider what he could have taught them instead. He is about to be made king of Judah. There is an obvious version of this moment in which the incoming man lets the old regime be remembered badly, and does not have to say a word to make it happen.

He composes a poem that honours Saul without qualification and orders it memorised.

The Book of Jashar is an older collection Israel drew on, cited once before in Joshua (Josh. 10:13) and lost to us. This poem survived because it was copied into Scripture.

'"Your glory, O Israel, is slain on your high places! How the mighty have fallen!"'

That last line is the refrain, and it comes three times — here, at verse 25, and again in the last verse. The poem is built around it.

'"Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult."'

The line has passed into the language, and most people who use it have no idea it is about the death of Saul.

What it means here is entirely concrete. Gath and Ashkelon are Philistine cities, and the runners have already gone out with the news — the previous chapter says so: they sent word to carry the good news to the house of their idols and to the people (1 Sam. 31:9). There will be dancing and singing in those streets tonight.

And David of all people knows what it looks like when the women of a city sing about a battle. He also knows Gath from the inside; he lived there for sixteen months, and before that he stood in its gateway drooling into his beard to stay alive.

'"You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew or rain upon you, nor fields of offerings! For there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, not anointed with oil."'

He curses the ground.

It is not a considered theological statement and it is not meant to be. Poetry does this. The mountain is where it happened, so let nothing grow there again — no dew, no rain, no crop good enough to bring to the altar.

Then the detail that carries the grief, and it is a piece of equipment.

The shield of Saul, not anointed with oil. A leather-faced shield was rubbed with oil to keep it supple and turn a blade, and it was part of a soldier's routine, done before a battle and after it. Saul's is lying on the mountain and nobody is going to oil it again.

That is how the poem says he is dead. Not a statement about the soul or the grave — a picture of good gear left out in the weather, ruined by neglect, because the man who looked after it is not coming back.

And there may be a second thing in the word. Anointed is the word the whole of 1 Samuel turns on, and it has been used of Saul over and over, and it is what David called him eight verses ago. Here it is, in its ordinary sense, about a shield.

'"From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan turned not back, and the sword of Saul returned not empty."'

Both men are praised as soldiers, and the praise is true.

Jonathan's bow. It is the right instrument to remember him by — it is the weapon he used to signal David in the field at Gibeah, on the day they parted (1 Sam. 20:20-22), and the poem is called the Song of the Bow.

'"Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely! In life and in death they were not divided; they were swifter than eagles; they were stronger than lions."'

Now that is generous past the facts, and it has to be said.

In life and in death they were not divided. They were divided. Saul threw a spear at Jonathan across a dinner table for defending David, and Jonathan left in fierce anger and did not eat (1 Sam. 20:33-34). Jonathan went behind his father's back repeatedly, made a covenant with the man his father was hunting, told that man he would have his father's throne, and said outright Saul my father also knows this.

David knew every bit of that. He was on the other end of most of it.

So what is he doing?

He is saying the largest true thing rather than the most exact one. In the end they were not divided: the son stood in his father's line on his father's mountain and died there with him, when he could have been somewhere else and had every reason to be. Whatever came between them, that is where Jonathan was on the last day.

This is not dishonesty, and the difference matters. He is not saying the household was happy. He is choosing, out of everything he could accurately report about a dead man, the part that is honourable — and he is doing it in a poem he intends the whole nation to memorise, about a king whose crown he is about to wear.

There is a discipline in that which most people have never attempted. Nearly everyone, given a grievance and an audience, will tell the exact truth in the shape that damages. David had more material than anybody and used none of it.

'"You daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you luxuriously in scarlet, who put ornaments of gold on your apparel."'

This verse should stop a reader, because of who is being addressed and what is being remembered.

The daughters of Israel are the women who came out of all the cities singing and dancing with tambourines — Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands (1 Sam. 18:7). That song made Saul watch him with a spear in his hand. It was quoted at him in Gath. It nearly cost him his life twice.

He calls those same women to weep for Saul.

And what he tells them to remember is the prosperity. Scarlet cloth and gold ornaments meant a country secure enough and rich enough for ordinary women to be well dressed — and that was Saul's doing. He beat the Philistines at Michmash and the Ammonites at Jabesh and the raiders on every side, and for forty years Israel had a king and an army and something in the barn.

It is the true good thing, and David goes looking for it and says it out loud.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–27 — Your Love to Me Was Extraordinary
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How the mighty have fallen in the midst of the battle! Jonathan lies slain on your high places (v. 25). Then the poem stops being public: I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women (v. 26). And the refrain a third time, with four words added: how the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war perished! (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The comparison is one of kinds, not of degrees within one kind. Jonathan and David were sworn brothers under a covenant made three times before the LORD, and the loyalty that held it — a king's heir handing over his own succession and dying for his father's cause anyway — is what David is measuring. It is hesed, and he says he has never met its equal.
verseByVerse.examples: Now read the whole poem again for two things that are not in it. There is not one word about David — no relief, no throne, no hint that the man who hunted him for years is conveniently dead. And there is not one mention of God, which is unusual for this writer. Scripture leaves the grief exactly as it came out.

verseByVerse.quote: "How the mighty have fallen in the midst of the battle! "Jonathan lies slain on your high places. I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women. "How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war perished!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"How the mighty have fallen in the midst of the battle! Jonathan lies slain on your high places."'

The refrain comes back, and then the poem narrows to one name.

'"I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women."'

Everything before this has been public. This is not.

I am distressed for you. The Hebrew is the language of a narrow place, of being pressed and constricted; it is grief as a physical pressure. And the address is personal: my brother. They were not brothers. They were brothers-in-law by a marriage that Saul dissolved by force, and they were brothers by covenant, which was the tie that held.

Very pleasant have you been to me. A small word doing a large job. Not useful, not loyal, though he was both past all reckoning. Pleasant. Being with him was good.

Then the line people stop at, and it deserves a plain answer rather than an argument.

Your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women.

The comparison is between kinds, not between degrees inside one kind. What Jonathan gave David was covenant loyalty — hesed, the word for love that keeps its promises after the reasons for keeping them have gone — and they had sworn it before the LORD three separate times.

Look at what it actually consisted of, because the poem is measuring something specific. The heir to the throne of Israel took off his own robe and armour and sword and belt and handed them to a shepherd (1 Sam. 18:4). He defended that shepherd to a king who threw a spear at him for it. He told him twice that the throne would be his and said I shall be next to you, which was a renunciation of everything he was born to. He walked into a wilderness his father's army was searching, for no purpose except to strengthen a frightened man's hand in God. And then he went home and died in his father's lost battle.

David is saying he never met anything like it anywhere else, and he had a wife who loved him and let him down through a window with a rope.

Nothing in the text or in the culture points this at anything other than what it says: a man grieving the friend who kept faith with him at the cost of a kingdom. Reading it otherwise requires importing a category the passage does not use and the ancient world did not employ this vocabulary for.

Notice instead that a king wrote it down, put his own grief in the first person, and had it taught to a nation — which is not a thing men in his position generally do in any century.

'"How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war perished!"'

The refrain a third time, with four words added, and the poem stops.

The weapons of war perished. The last line is about equipment again, as verse 21 was, and it means more than swords. The men who were Israel's defence are lying on a hill.

Now read the whole thing back, and look for two things that are not in it.

The first is David.

Twenty-seven verses, and there is not one word about what any of this means for him. No relief. No sense of an ending. Nothing about the throne he has been anointed for and waited years to receive, and no hint anywhere that the man who spent a decade trying to kill him is conveniently dead.

He has every reason to feel some of that and he is not a man who hides his feelings; the psalms are full of him saying exactly what is in him, including things people would rather he had not written down. Here there is nothing for himself at all. Whatever relief he felt, this is not where he put it.

The second absence is stranger.

There is no mention of God in the poem.

Not one. No the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away, no appeal, no theology of any kind. This from a man who cannot get through eight verses of a psalm without addressing God directly, and who has just spent an entire chapter defending the sanctity of the LORD's anointed.

Scripture keeps it exactly as it came out.

Anybody who has been made to feel that grief must be tidy or theological before it is permitted should sit with that. This is the man after God's own heart, and on the day the news came he wrote a poem full of scarlet cloth and eagles and an unoiled shield, with no doctrine in it and nothing about himself, and God preserved it in the canon.

Sometimes the godly thing is not to explain the loss. It is to say plainly how good the dead were and how much it hurts.

1.theology:
The lie, and why the reader can see it (vv. 6-10). His story contradicts an eyewitness account given one chapter earlier: Saul fell on his own sword, and the armour-bearer saw that Saul was dead before falling on his own (1 Sam. 31:4-5). Nobody is on a battlefield by chance. He stripped the insignia off a corpse and invented a part, having calculated that a rival claimant would pay not for the news but for the deed — which tells you exactly how he expected years of being hunted to have shaped a man.

An Amalekite (v. 8). Saul lost the kingdom over that nation at Gilgal, and Samuel named it at Endor as the reason for the disaster the next day (1 Sam. 15:1-23; 28:18). David has come to Ziklag straight from destroying the Amalekites who burned it. The writer puts the word in the man's own mouth and offers no comment, exactly as he did all through the last book.

The principle survives the arrival of power (v. 14). How is it you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed? is what he said in the cave at Engedi (1 Sam. 24:6) and to Abishai over the sleeping king (1 Sam. 26:9). He held it while hunted, hungry and living in caves, and argued his own men out of it twice. Almost anyone can keep a principle while it is costing them and feel righteous doing it; the test is the day it costs nothing and nobody would notice its absence.

Condemned by his mouth, not his deed (v. 16). David does not say you killed the king but you said you killed the king — and the act almost certainly never happened. A man who will invent a murder to advance himself has told you what he is, and he was given the account of himself he chose to give.

Grief put on the syllabus (v. 18). He could have said nothing and let the old regime be remembered badly, which requires no effort at all from an incoming king. Instead he writes a poem honouring Saul without qualification and has it taught to Judah, so that a whole generation's feeling about the dead king is shaped by his.

The unoiled shield (v. 21). Leather was rubbed with oil to stay supple and turn a blade. Saul's lies on the mountain and nobody will oil it again — which is how the poem says he is dead: not a statement about the grave but a picture of good gear left out in the weather because the man who looked after it is not coming back.

The largest true thing, not the most exact (v. 23). In life and in death they were not divided is generous past the facts; Saul threw a spear at Jonathan for defending David (1 Sam. 20:33). David knew all of it and was on the other end of most of it. He chooses, out of everything he could accurately report about a dead man, the part that is honourable — and it is true in the largest sense, because Jonathan stood in his father's line on his father's mountain when he had every reason to be elsewhere. Nearly anyone with a grievance and an audience will tell the exact truth in the shape that damages. David had more material than anybody and used none of it.

The scarlet and the gold (v. 24). He calls the very women who sang Saul his thousands, David his ten thousands — the song that put a spear in Saul's hand and nearly killed him twice — to weep for Saul; and what he gives them to remember is the prosperity. Forty years of a king and an army meant a country secure enough for ordinary women to be well dressed. He goes looking for the true good thing and says it out loud.

Surpassing the love of women (v. 26). The comparison is of kinds, not of degrees within a kind. What Jonathan gave was covenant hesed, sworn before the LORD three times: the heir to the throne handed over his robe, armour, sword and belt (1 Sam. 18:4), defended David to a king who speared at him for it, said I shall be next to you in renunciation of everything he was born to, and walked into a hunted wilderness for no purpose but to strengthen his friend's hand in God. Nothing in the text points anywhere else; reading it otherwise imports a category the passage does not use. What is remarkable is that a king wrote his own grief in the first person and had a nation learn it.

Two absences, and both are the point. Not one word about David — no relief, no throne, no hint that the man who hunted him for a decade is conveniently dead — from a writer who elsewhere says exactly what is in him, including things most people would not write down. And not one mention of God in the whole poem, which is extraordinary for this man. Scripture keeps it as it came, which matters a great deal to anybody made to feel that grief must be tidy or theological before it is permitted. Sometimes the godly thing is not to explain the loss but to say plainly how good the dead were and how much it hurts.
1.examples:
Then: A man walked three days across the Negeb carrying a dead king's crown and a story he had made up on the road, expecting to be paid for claiming a murder — and was executed on the strength of his own account by the one person in Israel who had twice refused to commit it when he had the chance.

Now: Two things. The Amalekite is a study in misreading somebody: he assumed that years of persecution had made David into the kind of man who would reward the news, and he built his whole approach on it. People will tell you what they think you are by what they think will please you. And the lament is the harder lesson. David had more accurate, damaging material about Saul than any person alive, an audience ready to hear it, and every political reason to let it out — and instead he went looking for what was genuinely good about the man and taught it to a nation. That is not the same as pretending. It is choosing which true thing to say.

2.title: Two Kings in Israel
2.text: <sup>1</sup>After this David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up." David said, "To which shall I go up?" And he said, "To Hebron."<sup>2</sup>So David went up there, and his two wives also, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel.<sup>3</sup>And David brought up his men who were with him, everyone with his household, and they lived in the towns of Hebron.<sup>4</sup>And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. When they told David, "It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul,"<sup>5</sup>David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, "May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him.<sup>6</sup>Now may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I will do good to you because you have done this thing.<sup>7</sup>Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."<sup>8</sup>But Abner the son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth the son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim,<sup>9</sup>and he made him king over Gilead and the Ashurites and Jezreel and Ephraim and Benjamin and all Israel.<sup>10</sup>Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David.<sup>11</sup>And the time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.<sup>12</sup>Abner the son of Ner, and the servants of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.<sup>13</sup>And Joab the son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. And they sat down, the one on the one side of the pool, and the other on the other side of the pool.<sup>14</sup>And Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men arise and compete before us." And Joab said, "Let them arise."<sup>15</sup>Then they arose and passed over by number, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David.<sup>16</sup>And each caught his opponent by the head and thrust his sword in his opponent's side, so they fell down together. Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which is at Gibeon.<sup>17</sup>And the battle was very fierce that day. And Abner and the men of Israel were beaten before the servants of David.<sup>18</sup>And the three sons of Zeruiah were there, Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was as swift of foot as a wild gazelle.<sup>19</sup>And Asahel pursued Abner, and as he went, he turned neither to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner.<sup>20</sup>Then Abner looked behind him and said, "Is it you, Asahel?" And he answered, "It is I."<sup>21</sup>Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right hand or to your left, and seize one of the young men and take his spoil." But Asahel would not turn aside from following him.<sup>22</sup>And Abner said again to Asahel, "Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?"<sup>23</sup>But he refused to turn aside. Therefore Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, so that the spear came out at his back. And he fell there and died where he was. And all who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died, stood still.<sup>24</sup>But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. And as the sun was going down they came to the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon.<sup>25</sup>And the people of Benjamin gathered themselves together behind Abner and became one group and took their stand on the top of a hill.<sup>26</sup>Then Abner called to Joab, "Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? How long will it be before you tell your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers?"<sup>27</sup>And Joab said, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely the men would not have given up the pursuit of their brothers until the morning."<sup>28</sup>So Joab blew the trumpet, and all the men stopped and pursued Israel no more, nor did they fight anymore.<sup>29</sup>And Abner and his men went all that night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, and marching the whole morning, they came to Mahanaim.<sup>30</sup>Joab returned from the pursuit of Abner. And when he had gathered all the people together, there were missing from David's servants nineteen men besides Asahel.<sup>31</sup>But the servants of David had struck down of Benjamin 360 of Abner's men.<sup>32</sup>And they took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was at Bethlehem. And Joab and his men marched all night, and the day broke upon them at Hebron.
2.overview:
Four words open the chapter and they are the difference between this king and the last one: David inquired of the LORD. He is holding the dead king's crown, he has Samuel's anointing behind him, Saul and his heir are dead and the northern army is destroyed — and there is no living person whose permission he needs. He asks anyway. Then, given a yes, he asks a second question rather than let the first answer cover it. Set that against David said in his heart at 1 Sam. 27:1, which cost him sixteen months in enemy country.

His first act as king is a thank-you letter to Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul — the town that walked all night through occupied territory to take four bodies off a Philistine wall, because of one night forty years earlier when the Spirit came on a young man behind a plough. David names what they did with the covenant word and asks God to do the same for them. It is entirely genuine, and it also tells the north exactly what kind of king has been crowned in the south. Godly and shrewd are not opposites; they are just harder to hold together than either alone.

Then the pool of Gibeon, and both armies are Israelite. Abner proposes a contest to keep a war small, and all twenty-four champions grab each other by the head and die in the same second, settling nothing — so the armies fight anyway. Asahel, who could run, chases the enemy commander in a straight line; Abner warns him twice, offers him an honourable way out, and finally jabs backwards with the blunt end of his spear to wind him. It goes straight through. Abner was still trying not to kill him at the moment he killed him.

And the best line of the day comes from the man most responsible for it: shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? Three hundred and eighty Israelites are dead at a water tank. Both armies then march all night in opposite directions, and nothing has been decided.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — David Inquired of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After this David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?" The answer is yes; he asks a second question — to which shall I go up? — and is told Hebron (v. 1). He goes up with his two wives and every man and household, and the men of Judah anoint him king over the house of Judah (vv. 2-4). Told that it was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul, he sends them a blessing: may you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him... may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: He has the dead king's crown in his hands, an anointing from Samuel behind him, and a claim nobody could argue with — and he asks. Then, given a yes, he asks again rather than treat the first answer as covering the second. Set that beside 1 Sam. 27:1, where he said in his heart and moved six hundred families into enemy country for sixteen months.
verseByVerse.examples: And his first recorded act as king is a thank-you letter to the town that buried Saul. He uses the covenant word for what they did — the love that keeps going after the reason for it has gone — and asks God to show them the same. It is genuine, and it also tells every man in the north exactly what kind of king has just been crowned in the south.

verseByVerse.quote: After this David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up." David said, "To which shall I go up?" And he said, "To Hebron." So David went up there, and his two wives also, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel. And David brought up his men who were with him, everyone with his household, and they lived in the towns of Hebron. And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. When they told David, "It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul," David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, "May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him. Now may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I will do good to you because you have done this thing. Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After this David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up." David said, "To which shall I go up?" And he said, "To Hebron."'

Four words open the book's second chapter and they are the whole difference between this man and the last one: David inquired of the LORD.

Consider what he is holding while he asks.

He has the crown of the dead king, brought to him by the Amalekite. He has Samuel's anointing from a courtyard in Bethlehem years ago. Saul is dead, his heir is dead, and the northern army is destroyed. He has six hundred men, a reputation, and the tribe of Judah waiting. Nobody in the country could argue with the claim, and there is no living person he needs permission from.

He asks anyway.

And then he does something more instructive still. He gets a yes — go up — and he does not run with it. He asks a second question: to which shall I go up?

He will not treat the first answer as covering the second. Permission to move is not instruction about where, and he is not going to fill the gap himself and call the whole thing guidance.

Now set this against the last time we watched him make a large decision. Then David said in his heart, "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines" (1 Sam. 27:1). No priest, no ephod, no prophet — and all three were in the camp. That sentence cost him sixteen months in enemy country and a page of his life he could not undo.

Same man. Opposite move. The difference is Ziklag: he asked for the ephod standing in the ashes of his own town (1 Sam. 30:7), and he has not stopped since.

Hebron is the right answer and he could not have known it. It is the oldest covenant ground in the country — Abraham bought the field and the cave there and buried Sarah in it, and Abraham and Isaac and Jacob are all in that ground (Gen. 23; 49:31). It is a Levitical city and a city of refuge, and it sits in the hill country at the centre of Judah's territory.

He is not told why. He is told where.

'So David went up there, and his two wives also, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel. And David brought up his men who were with him, every man with his household, and they lived in the towns of Hebron.'

Six hundred households move at once, and the writer counts the wives.

Abigail is here, who came down a mountain track with two hundred loaves and talked him out of a massacre. Ahinoam is here. Michal, his first wife, is not: Saul gave her to another man while David was in the wilderness, and getting her back is going to be a condition in the next chapter.

'And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah.'

The third anointing, and each one has been from a different quarter.

Samuel poured the oil in his father's house in front of seven passed-over brothers, and nobody outside that room knew (1 Sam. 16:13). Now his own tribe does it publicly. And seven and a half years from now the elders of all Israel will come to Hebron and do it a third time (5:3).

God keeps confirming the same thing in front of larger and larger audiences, and each confirmation arrives only when the man has waited for it.

'When they told David, "It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul,"'

'David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, "May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him."'

His first recorded act as king is a thank-you letter to the men who buried his enemy.

Remember what they did. Jabesh-gilead is across the Jordan; Beth-shan, where Saul's body was nailed to the wall, is Philistine-held. Those men walked all night through occupied country, took four bodies down off a public wall, carried them home, burned them, buried the bones under a tamarisk and fasted for a week — for a king who had been failing them for years, with no possible reward, at real risk (1 Sam. 31:11-13).

And they did it because of one night forty years earlier, when Saul was a young man behind a plough and the Spirit of God rushed on him and he marched all night to save their town from an Ammonite who wanted every right eye in it (1 Sam. 11).

David sees exactly what that was and names it.

'"Now may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I will do good to you because you have done this thing."'

Steadfast love and faithfulness. The first word is hesed — the covenant word, love that keeps its promises when the reasons for keeping them have gone. It is what Jonathan asked David to show his descendants. It is what Abigail's whole speech turned on. It is what Jabesh-gilead did.

He asks God to do to them what they did to Saul.

'"Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."'

And then, at the end, the politics — and it would be dishonest to pretend it is not there.

He tells them Saul is dead and that Judah has crowned him, and he does not ask them for anything. That last sentence is information delivered to the most fiercely pro-Saul town in the country, by a man who has just praised them for their loyalty to Saul, and every word of it is calculated.

Both things are true at once, and the text is comfortable with that. The gratitude is real — he wrote a lament for Saul nobody made him write. And he is also a man who understands that the north is watching to see whether the new king in the south regards them as the enemy, and he has chosen the one gesture that answers the question before it is asked.

Godly and shrewd are not opposites. They are simply harder to hold together than either one on its own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — Let the Young Men Compete Before Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abner takes Saul's surviving son Ish-bosheth across the Jordan to Mahanaim and makes him king over the north, while Judah follows David (vv. 8-10). Seven and a half years at Hebron (v. 11). The two forces meet at the pool of Gibeon and sit down on opposite sides of it (vv. 12-13). Abner proposes a contest: let the young men arise and compete before us (v. 14). Twelve against twelve step out — and each caught his opponent by the head and thrust his sword in his opponent's side, so they fell down together (vv. 15-16). The place is named the Field of Sword-Edges, and the battle was very fierce that day (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Both armies are Israelite. This is a civil war, and the men on either side of that pool were in the same muster a month ago. Ish-bosheth is a cipher — he makes one complaint in the whole book and is murdered in bed — and Abner is the kingdom.
verseByVerse.examples: The contest is a device for limiting a war, and twenty-four men kill each other simultaneously and settle nothing. That is what the place-name commemorates. Then the real fighting starts, and it runs for years.

verseByVerse.quote: But Abner the son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth the son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim, and he made him king over Gilead and the Ashurites and Jezreel and Ephraim and Benjamin and all Israel. Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David. And the time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months. Abner the son of Ner, and the servants of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon. And Joab the son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. And they sat down, the one on the one side of the pool, and the other on the other side of the pool. And Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men arise and compete before us." And Joab said, "Let them arise." Then they arose and passed over by number, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David. And each caught his opponent by the head and thrust his sword in his opponent's side, so they fell down together. Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which is at Gibeon. And the battle was very fierce that day. And Abner and the men of Israel were beaten before the servants of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But Abner the son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth the son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim, and he made him king over Gilead and the Ashurites and Jezreel and Ephraim and Benjamin and all Israel.'

Read the verbs. Abner took him, brought him over, and made him king.

Ish-bosheth does nothing in that sentence, and he does very little in the rest of the book. He speaks once, makes an accusation that destroys his own kingdom, and is murdered asleep in the afternoon. Abner is the reality; the son of Saul is the paperwork.

Note also where they go: Mahanaim, on the far side of the Jordan. The heartland is not safe enough to be crowned in.

'Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David. And the time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.'

Two years against seven and a half, and the arithmetic is doing something.

Ish-bosheth's reign is short and David's Hebron years are long, which means most of that period had no rival king in it at all. There is a gap the writer does not explain, and the effect is that David sat in Hebron for the better part of eight years as king of one tribe out of twelve, waiting. He had been waiting for about fifteen years already.

'Abner the son of Ner, servant of Ish-bosheth, and the servants of David went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon. And Joab the son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. And they sat down, the one on the one side of the pool, and the other on the other side of the pool.'

Two armies sit down on opposite sides of a water tank and look at each other.

The pool at Gibeon has been dug out by archaeologists — a great shaft cut down through rock, with a spiral stair inside it, wide enough to be a landmark. It is a real place and this is a real afternoon, and the picture the sentence makes is of men waiting for somebody to decide something.

And they are all Israelites. That is the fact to keep hold of through this entire chapter and the next. Every man on both sides of that pool is a son of Jacob; some of them fought in the same line at Michmash. Joab is David's nephew and Abner is Saul's cousin, and the war they are about to start is a family quarrel with armies.

'And Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men arise and compete before us." And Joab said, "Let them arise."'

The word is the ordinary one for a game.

What Abner proposes is a representative contest — a fixed number of champions from each side, the result standing for the whole. It was a recognised way of settling a matter without committing two armies, and everyone in the region understood it. Goliath had proposed exactly this in the Valley of Elah, and it had worked (1 Sam. 17:8-9).

So the intention is not bloodthirsty. Two generals who both know this war cannot really be won are looking for a way to keep the cost down.

Hold that, because of what happens next.

'Then they arose and passed over by number, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David.'

'And each caught his opponent by the head and thrust his sword in his opponent's side, so they fell down together. Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which is at Gibeon.'

All twenty-four die at once.

Read the sentence again, because it is one of the more terrible pieces of writing in the book and it is doing it entirely with choreography. Each man grabs his opposite number by the head and puts a sword in his side, and they go down in pairs. There is no winner. There is not even a fight worth describing. Twenty-four young men take hold of each other and die together in the same second.

Helkath-hazzurim means something like the Field of Sword-Edges, and Israel put that name on the ground and kept it.

Now think about what has just happened to Abner's plan. He proposed a contest to avoid a battle. The contest produced twenty-four dead and settled absolutely nothing, because there was nothing to settle — both teams lost.

'And the battle was very fierce that day. And Abner and the men of Israel were beaten before the servants of David.'

So the armies go in anyway.

That is what came of the sensible plan for limiting the damage: the deaths of the twenty-four, and then the general engagement they were supposed to prevent, and then a war that runs for years.

There is a whole class of human decision in this. A measure adopted to contain a conflict becomes the thing that ignites it, because the men involved were never actually willing to accept a result they did not like. Abner would not have gone home if his twelve had lost. Neither would Joab. The tournament was a fiction they both agreed to while the swords were still sheathed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — Turn Aside from Following Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asahel, Joab's brother, is as swift of foot as a wild gazelle, and he goes straight for Abner and will not turn to right or left (vv. 18-19). Abner tells him twice to break off — turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab? (vv. 21-22). He will not. So Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, and the spear came out at his back. And he fell there and died where he was (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Abner is the most experienced soldier in Israel and he does not want this killing. He warns the boy twice, offers him an easier target, and names the exact reason: how could I lift up my face to your brother Joab? He can see the whole feud coming.
verseByVerse.examples: The blow is struck with the wrong end of the spear — a shove meant to wind a man and stop him, driven home by his own speed. It goes through him. That accident is the fuse for the murder at the gate in the next chapter, and for Joab's own execution forty years later (1 Kings 2:5-6).

verseByVerse.quote: And the three sons of Zeruiah were there, Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was as swift of foot as a wild gazelle. And Asahel pursued Abner, and as he went, he turned neither to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner. Then Abner looked behind him and said, "Is it you, Asahel?" And he answered, "It is I." Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right hand or to your left, and seize one of the young men and take his spoil." But Asahel would not turn aside from following him. And Abner said again to Asahel, "Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?" But he refused to turn aside. Therefore Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, so that the spear came out at his back. And he fell there and died where he was. And all who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died, stood still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the three sons of Zeruiah were there, Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was as swift of foot as a wild gazelle.'

The three brothers are named together, and they are David's nephews — Zeruiah is his sister. Between them they will run his army, win his wars, and cause him more trouble than any of his enemies.

Asahel is introduced by the one thing everybody knew about him. He could run.

'And Asahel pursued Abner, and as he went, he turned neither to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner.'

He picks the commander-in-chief of the opposing army and goes after him in a straight line.

The phrase neither to the right hand nor to the left is normally a compliment in Scripture; it is what is said of a king who keeps the law. Here it describes a young man who has decided on a target and will not be talked out of it.

'Then Abner looked behind him and said, "Is it you, Asahel?" And he answered, "It is I."'

Abner knows him by name. Of course he does — a month ago they were in the same country and possibly the same army, and everyone knew who the fast one was.

'Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right hand or to your left, and seize one of the young men and take his spoil." But Asahel would not turn aside from following him.'

The first warning, and note the shape of it: not go home but take somebody else. He is offering the boy an honourable way out with plunder in his hands, so that nothing has to be explained afterwards.

'And Abner said again to Asahel, "Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?"'

The second warning, and the reason given is the whole future of the book.

How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?

Abner is the most experienced soldier alive in Israel and he can see exactly what is coming. Not the tactical situation — he could kill this boy in a second and both of them know it — but what follows. Blood between families does not stay where it falls. If he kills Asahel, Joab will come for him, and it will not matter what the circumstances were.

He is not begging for his life. He is warning a young man that his death will start something neither of them can stop.

And Asahel keeps running.

'So Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, and the spear came out at his back. And he fell there and died where he was.'

With the butt of his spear.

That detail is the whole of Abner's intention and it is easy to read past. He does not turn and put the point through him. He jabs backwards with the blunt end — the counterweight at the base of the shaft — which is what you do to wind a man, knock the breath out of him, and stop him without killing him.

And it goes straight through, because Asahel was running flat out and ran onto it. The spear comes out at his back.

Abner was still trying not to kill him at the moment he killed him.

'And all who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died, stood still.'

The pursuit stops. Men come round the shoulder of the hill, see who is lying there, and cannot go on.

That single line does more than a paragraph of description. Everyone who arrives knows the face, knows whose brother he is, and understands in the same instant what has just been set in motion.

Because this is the fuse. Everything that happens to Abner in the next chapter happens because of this afternoon: Joab will call him aside at the gate of Hebron as though to speak with him privately, and put a blade in his stomach — the same wound, in the same place, returned.

And that murder is not the end of it either. Forty years later, dying, David will still be talking about it, and will tell Solomon what to do about Joab: you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war (1 Kings 2:5-6). Joab dies holding the horns of the altar.

All of it comes out of a boy who could run fast and would not turn aside.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–32 — Shall the Sword Devour Forever?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab and Abishai pursue until sundown, and Abner's men rally on a hilltop (vv. 24-25). Then Abner calls down: shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? How long will you refrain from telling your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers? (v. 26). Joab answers that if he had not spoken, the pursuit would have gone on till morning — blows the trumpet, and stops (vv. 27-28). Abner marches all night back across the Jordan (v. 29). The count: nineteen of David's men and Asahel; three hundred and sixty of Abner's (vv. 30-31). They bury Asahel at Bethlehem and march all night to Hebron (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: The pursuit of their brothers. Abner names what this is, and he is the man who started it that morning with a proposal for a tournament. The best sentence in the chapter comes from the person most responsible for the day.
verseByVerse.examples: Both sides then march all night in opposite directions, one to a burial at Bethlehem and one across the Jordan. Nothing has been decided and three hundred and eighty-one Israelites are dead.

verseByVerse.quote: But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. And as the sun was going down they came to the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon. And the people of Benjamin gathered themselves together behind Abner and became one group and took their stand on the top of a hill. Then Abner called to Joab, "Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? How long will it be before you tell your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers?" And Joab said, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely the men would not have given up the pursuit of their brothers until the morning." So Joab blew the trumpet, and all the men stopped and pursued Israel no more, nor did they fight anymore. And Abner and his men went all that night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, and marching the whole morning, they came to Mahanaim. Joab returned from the pursuit of Abner. And when he had gathered all the people together, there were missing from David's servants nineteen men besides Asahel. But the servants of David had struck down of Benjamin 360 of Abner's men. And they took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was at Bethlehem. And Joab and his men marched all night, and the day broke upon them at Hebron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. And as the sun was going down they came to the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon.'

The dead brother's two brothers keep going, and the chase runs all afternoon.

'And the people of Benjamin gathered themselves together behind Abner and became one group and took their stand on the top of a hill.'

Abner's men rally, and the pursuit has now caught up with a formed body on high ground, which means the next thing will be expensive for everybody.

'Then Abner called to Joab, "Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? How long will you refrain from telling your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers?"'

That is the best thing anybody says in this chapter, and it comes out of the mouth of the man who caused the day.

Take it in three parts.

Shall the sword devour forever? The picture is of a weapon that eats — a thing with an appetite of its own that does not stop when the reason for drawing it has been met. Anybody who has watched a quarrel outlive its cause knows the image is exact.

Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? He is not appealing to mercy. He is telling a professional soldier something a professional soldier already knows: this ends badly for your side too, and the taste of it lasts.

The pursuit of their brothers.

There is the word, and it is the true description of the whole day. Not enemies. Brothers. The men on that hill and the men at the bottom of it are the same nation, and everybody has been pretending otherwise since breakfast.

Now the honesty the passage requires. Abner started this. He proposed the contest at the pool that morning; twenty-four young men are dead because of a suggestion he made; and he has spent the afternoon losing a battle he chose to fight. He is also, at this precise moment, calling for peace from a hilltop because he is about to be overrun.

All of that is true, and the sentence is still true. Right words are not always spoken by disinterested people, and self-interest does not automatically make a thing false. Abner is manoeuvring, and he is also correct, and Joab knows it.

'And Joab said, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely the men would not have given up the pursuit of their brothers until the morning."'

Joab's answer is colder than it looks, and it repays a second reading.

He does not disagree. He picks up Abner's own phrase — the pursuit of their brothers — and says that if Abner had not spoken, it would have gone on all night.

Which is either a complaint or a confession, and probably both. He is saying: I would not have stopped. You stopped me. And there is not a word in it about Asahel, from a man who has just spent the afternoon chasing the person who killed his brother, and who will settle that account in the next chapter with a knife.

'So Joab blew the trumpet, and all the men stopped and pursued Israel no more, nor did they fight anymore.'

He stops it, and he stops it immediately. Whatever else is true of Joab — and a great deal is — he is not a man who loses control of himself or his troops.

'And Abner and his men went all night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, and marching the whole morning, they came to Mahanaim.'

'Joab returned from the pursuit of Abner. And when he had gathered all the people together, there were missing from David's servants nineteen men besides Asahel. But the servants of David had struck down of Benjamin 360 of Abner's men.'

The count is given, and the writer counts both sides.

Nineteen and Asahel. Three hundred and sixty. Three hundred and eighty Israelites dead in one afternoon at a water tank, and one name among them — because that is the one that will cost more than all the rest put together.

Note that David's side won convincingly, nearly nineteen to one. It changed nothing. There will be another five or six years of this.

'And they took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was at Bethlehem. And Joab and his men marched all night, and the day broke upon them at Hebron.'

The chapter ends with two night marches going in opposite directions.

Abner is crossing the Jordan in the dark to get home to Mahanaim. Joab is carrying his brother's body to Bethlehem, burying him in their father's tomb, and then walking through the night to Hebron, and the sun comes up on him as he arrives.

Both armies spend the same night walking away from a battle that decided nothing. It is a bleak, exact ending, and the writer offers no comment on any of it.

The kingdom is coming to David. This is what it costs while it comes, and most of the cost is being paid by people who never chose either side.

2.theology:
He asks, and then he asks again (v. 1). The claim was unarguable and the moment was obvious, and he still put it to God — and having been told go up, he would not treat that as an answer to where. Permission to move is not instruction about direction, and he refuses to fill the gap himself and call the result guidance. The contrast is exact and the writer means it: 1 Sam. 27:1, David said in his heart, with a priest, an ephod and a prophet all sitting in his own camp. What changed was Ziklag, where he called for the ephod standing in the ashes.

Hebron, and being told where but not why (v. 1). It is the oldest covenant ground in the country — Abraham's purchased field, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob all buried in it (Gen. 23; 49:31) — a Levitical city and a city of refuge at the centre of Judah. He could not have reasoned his way to it, and he is given the destination without the argument for it.

Three anointings, each to a wider audience (v. 4). Samuel's oil in a private house that nobody outside the room knew about (1 Sam. 16:13); now his own tribe, publicly; and in seven and a half years the elders of all Israel at this same Hebron (5:3). God keeps confirming the same word in front of larger audiences, and each confirmation arrives only after the waiting.

The thank-you to Jabesh-gilead (vv. 5-7). He uses hesed of what they did and asks God to show them the same — and then, at the end, tells them Saul is dead and Judah has crowned him, which is a political sentence delivered to the most pro-Saul town in Israel. Both are true at once and the text is comfortable with it. The gratitude is real; he wrote a lament nobody made him write. He is also a man who knows the north is watching, and who picks the one gesture that answers the question before it is asked.

Abner is the kingdom (vv. 8-10). Read the verbs: Abner took Ish-bosheth, brought him over, made him king. The son of Saul speaks once in the whole book, destroys his own throne with the sentence, and is murdered asleep in the afternoon. And they are crowned at Mahanaim, across the Jordan, because the heartland is not safe.

A measure to contain a war becomes the thing that starts it (vv. 14-17). Representative combat was a recognised way of settling a matter without two armies — Goliath had proposed it in the Valley of Elah. Here twenty-four men catch each other by the head and go down in pairs in the same second, and there is no winner and nothing settled, so the armies engage anyway. The tournament was a fiction both generals agreed to while the swords were sheathed; neither would have gone home on a losing result.

Abner did not want to kill him (vv. 21-23). Two warnings, an honourable alternative with plunder attached, and a reason stated out loud — how then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?
