7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the king lived in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies,<sup>2</sup>the king said to Nathan the prophet, "See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent."<sup>3</sup>And Nathan said to the king, "Go, do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you."<sup>4</sup>But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan,<sup>5</sup>"Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: Would you build me a house to dwell in?<sup>6</sup>I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt to this day, but I have been moving about in a tent for my dwelling.<sup>7</sup>In all places where I have moved with all the people of Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'<sup>8</sup>Now, therefore, thus you shall say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, that you should be prince over my people Israel.<sup>9</sup>And I have been with you wherever you went and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a great name, like the name of the great ones of the earth.<sup>10</sup>And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, so that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall afflict them no more, as formerly,<sup>11</sup>from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies. Moreover, the LORD declares to you that the LORD will make you a house.<sup>12</sup>When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom.<sup>13</sup>He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.<sup>14</sup>I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men, with the stripes of the sons of men,<sup>15</sup>but my steadfast love will not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away from before you.<sup>16</sup>And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever.'"<sup>17</sup>In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.<sup>18</sup>Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?<sup>19</sup>And yet this was a small thing in your eyes, O Lord GOD. You have spoken also of your servant's house for a great while to come, and this is instruction for mankind, O Lord GOD!<sup>20</sup>And what more can David say to you? For you know your servant, O Lord GOD!<sup>21</sup>Because of your promise, and according to your own heart, you have brought about all this greatness, to make your servant know it.<sup>22</sup>Therefore you are great, O Lord GOD. For there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.<sup>23</sup>And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making himself a name and doing for them great and awesome things by driving out before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, a nation and its gods?<sup>24</sup>And you established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever. And you, O LORD, became their God.<sup>25</sup>And now, O LORD God, confirm forever the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house, and do as you have spoken.<sup>26</sup>And your name will be magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts is God over Israel,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you.<sup>27</sup>For you, O LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have made this revelation to your servant, saying, 'I will build you a house.' Therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you.<sup>28</sup>And now, O Lord GOD, you are God, and your words are true, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.<sup>29</sup>Now therefore may it please you to bless the house of your servant, so that it may continue forever before you. For you, O Lord GOD, have spoken, and with your blessing shall the house of your servant be blessed forever."
7.overview:
For the first time in his life there is nothing trying to kill him. The Philistines are broken, the tribes are united, the ark is home, and the king is sitting in a house of Hiram's cedar — and what troubles him is that God's throne is still under canvas two hundred yards away. He does not propose anything. He states two facts side by side and leaves them there.

Nathan says go, do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you, and Nathan is wrong. He is a genuine prophet — the man who will say you are the man in this same room five chapters from now — and what he gives here is his own judgment about a plainly godly proposal, and God corrects it before morning. That distinction, drawn in consecutive verses, is worth more than most of what gets said about guidance.

And God's answer is that he never asked. I have been moving about in a tent — by choice, since Egypt — and in four centuries of judges he never once reproached anybody for the accommodation. Then the pivot, done with a single word used twice: David said I will build you a house and meant a temple; God says the LORD will make you a house and means a dynasty. A man offers a building and is given a family that does not end.

The promise runs on two levels and both are required. Solomon builds the temple and is disciplined; and forever occurs three times in five verses, and the New Testament reaches back for this passage with total confidence — Gabriel to Mary, Peter at Pentecost, Hebrews quoting verse 14 of Christ. And as I took it from Saul is the clause that changes everything: sin will meet the rod, and the covenant love will not be withdrawn. Then David goes in and sits down, which is not how Israelites prayed, and asks for nothing at all for seven verses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Would You Build Me a House to Dwell In?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king has rest from all his enemies, and says to Nathan: see now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent (vv. 1-2). Nathan answers at once — go, do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you (v. 3). But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan (v. 4), and it reverses him: would you build me a house to dwell in? I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt... but I have been moving about in a tent (vv. 5-6). And the question that settles it: did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel... saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?" (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Nathan is a true prophet and he is wrong. What he gives David is his own judgment — good judgment, generously offered, about a plainly godly proposal — and it is not the word of God, and God corrects it before morning. That distinction is worth more than most of what is said about guidance.
verseByVerse.examples: God has never asked for a house. He has been moving with his people since Egypt, in a tent, by choice, and in four centuries of judges he never once complained about the accommodation.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the king lived in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies, the king said to Nathan the prophet, "See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent." And Nathan said to the king, "Go, do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you." But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan, "Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: Would you build me a house to dwell in? I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt to this day, but I have been moving about in a tent for my dwelling. In all places where I have moved with all the people of Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now when the king lived in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies,'

Rest. It is the first time that word can be used about Israel in this book.

The Philistines are broken from Geba to Gezer, the civil war is over, the tribes are united, the capital is taken and the ark is home. For the first time in the man's life there is nothing immediately trying to kill him, and he has a house with a roof on it.

What a person does with that is revealing, and what David does with it is the subject of the greatest chapter in the book.

'the king said to Nathan the prophet, "See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent."'

He looks around his own sitting room and is uncomfortable.

The cedar is Hiram's, sent up from Tyre with the carpenters and masons who built the place (5:11). It is the finest building material in the ancient near east and it came as a gift, and David is now sitting in the result of it while the throne of God stands under canvas about two hundred yards away.

Note what he does not say. He does not propose anything, does not ask for permission, does not lay out a plan. He states the two facts side by side and leaves them there, and Nathan understands him perfectly.

This is the man at his best. His first thought when the pressure comes off is not what to do with the peace but that God's honour is lagging behind his own comfort.

'And Nathan said to the king, "Go, do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you."'

Nathan is wrong.

Stop on this, because it is easy to read past and it is one of the most useful verses in Scripture on the subject of guidance.

Nathan is a genuine prophet. He is not a court flatterer and not a fraud; he is the man who will walk into this same room five chapters from now and say you are the man to a king who has just had someone murdered. He has the courage and he has the office.

And here he gives an answer straight away, and it is his own opinion.

Look at how good the opinion is. The proposal is godly. The motive is pure. The man making it is the LORD's anointed, at the height of his obedience, in a season of obvious divine blessing. Every indicator points the same way. Nathan says what any wise and godly counsellor would say, and adds the clincher: the LORD is with you.

All of it is true, and the conclusion is wrong.

'But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan,'

God corrects him before morning, which is a kindness to both of them.

Here is what this establishes, and it should be held clearly. There is a difference between good counsel and the word of God, and the difference is not the godliness of the counsellor. A prophet speaking his own mind is a wise man speaking his own mind. When he speaks for God the text says so, and it says so here in a way that distinguishes the two in consecutive verses.

Which means several things at once. It means that the LORD is with you is not a guarantee that any particular plan is his. It means that a proposal can be sincerely devout, strategically sound, endorsed by a genuinely spiritual man, and still not be what God wants. And it means the check on all of it is not the quality of the advisers but whether God has actually said.

Nathan's willingness to come back the next day and reverse himself in front of the king is worth its own sentence. He does not defend his first answer or quietly let it stand. Verse 17 says he told David all these words, which included the correction of what Nathan himself had said the day before.

'"Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: Would you build me a house to dwell in?'"'

The question is not a rebuke, and the tone matters.

Nothing in what follows says David was wrong to want this, and a great deal in it says God is pleased with him. What the question does is turn the whole proposal over. Would you build me a house? — you, build, me.

'"I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt to this day, but I have been moving about in a tent for my dwelling."'

This is God's own account of the last four hundred years and it is startling.

I have been moving about in a tent.

He is not saying he was homeless or badly served. He is saying that this was the arrangement he chose. The tabernacle was designed to be taken down, carried and put up again, because the people it belonged to were going somewhere and God intended to go with them. Through the wilderness, into the land, through the whole disorder of the judges, God travelled.

A house is a good thing and it is a stationary thing. What God is pointing out, gently, is that he has never wanted to be housed.

'"In all places where I have moved with all the people of Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying, 'Why have you not built me a house of cedar?'"'

There is the sentence that settles the matter. He never asked.

Four centuries of Israelite leaders — Othniel, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, Samuel — and not one of them was ever told that God wanted a permanent building, or reproached for not providing one. The whole idea is David's, and God is pointing out, without heat, that it did not come from him.

That is a thing worth sitting still with. It is entirely possible to want something for God that God has not asked for, and to want it out of real love, and to be wrong. The test of a plan is not how much devotion went into it.

One more thing belongs here, because this chapter does not supply it and readers ask.

Why can David not build the temple? Nothing in 2 Samuel 7 says. The reason is given later, twice, in David's own mouth: the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "You have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name, because you have shed so much blood before me on the earth" (1 Chron. 22:8; and again 28:3).

The man who secured the land by war is not the man who builds the house of peace. His son will, and his son's name means peace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — The LORD Will Make You a House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The answer begins with biography: I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, that you should be prince over my people Israel; I have been with you wherever you went; I have cut off your enemies; I will make you a great name (vv. 8-9). Then the pivot: the LORD declares to you that the LORD will make you a house (v. 11). When your days are fulfilled... I will raise up your offspring after you... He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men... but my steadfast love will not depart from him, as I took it from Saul (vv. 12-15). And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever (v. 16). Nathan tells him all of it (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Count the pronouns in verses 8-11. I took, I have been with you, I have cut off, I will make, I will appoint, I will plant, I will give you rest, the LORD will make you a house. David offered to do something for God, and the reply is a list of what God has done and will do for him.
verseByVerse.examples: As I took it from Saul is the clause that makes this a different kind of thing from Saul's kingship. Sin will be met with discipline — the rod of men, real and painful and coming in chapter 12 — but the covenant love does not get withdrawn. That is the difference between being under discipline and being removed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, therefore, thus you shall say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, that you should be prince over my people Israel. And I have been with you wherever you went and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a great name, like the name of the great ones of the earth. And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, so that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall afflict them no more, as formerly, from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies. Moreover, the LORD declares to you that the LORD will make you a house. When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men, with the stripes of the sons of men, but my steadfast love will not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away from before you. And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever.'" In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"Now, therefore, thus you shall say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, that you should be prince over my people Israel.'"'

The answer to David's offer begins with David's biography, and the first two words are the whole of it.

I took you.

From the pasture. From following the sheep. That is where the messenger found him on the day Samuel came to Bethlehem — the eighth son, not called in, out with the flock because somebody had to be, while seven older brothers stood in the house being looked over.

God is reminding a man in a cedar palace where he was standing when this started, and he is doing it right before making him the largest promise in the Old Testament.

'"And I have been with you wherever you went and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a great name, like the name of the great ones of the earth."'

Now start counting, because the counting is the point.

I took you. I have been with you. I have cut off. I will make for you a great name. And it goes on: I will appoint a place for my people, I will plant them, I will give you rest, the LORD will make you a house.

David came into this conversation offering to do something for God. The reply is a recital in which God is the subject of every verb.

And a great name is not a throwaway. There are two other places in Scripture where that phrase matters. At Babel, men said let us make a name for ourselves, and were scattered (Gen. 11:4). To Abram, God said I will make your name great, and the whole covenant followed (Gen. 12:2). A great name is a thing men grasp at and God gives, and it never works the first way.

'"And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, so that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall afflict them no more, as formerly,"'

Before God says anything about David's house, he talks about the people.

That order keeps recurring. The kingdom was exalted for the sake of his people Israel (5:12); David is prince over my people Israel; and here the promise of security is Israel's before it is the king's. The dynasty exists for the nation, not the nation for the dynasty.

'"Moreover, the LORD declares to you that the LORD will make you a house."'

There is the turn, and it is done with a single word used twice.

The Hebrew is bayit, and it does the same double duty as the English house. It means a building. It also means a family line — the house of Saul, the house of David, which is how the writer has been using it for six chapters.

David said: I will build you a bayit. He meant a temple.

God says: I will build you a bayit. He means a dynasty.

The whole chapter is inside that exchange. A man offers God a building and is told he is going to be given a family that does not end. He came to give and is comprehensively out-given, which is the recurring experience of anybody who tries to do something for God.

'"When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom."'

'"He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever."'

Now the promise begins operating on two levels at once, and both of them are real, and neither one can be dropped.

The immediate level is Solomon. He is the offspring who comes from David's body, he does build the house, and Kings records the completion of it in exactly these terms (1 Kings 8:20). Everything in verses 12 to 15 has a first, plain, historical reference to the son who succeeds him.

And then there is a word that does not fit a man. Forever. It occurs three times in five verses, and it is not the language of a normal succession.

'"I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men, with the stripes of the sons of men,"'

Two halves of that verse, and they pull in different directions.

I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. That is adoption language, and it is the formula by which a king in Israel is declared God's own son. Psalm 2 uses it: you are my Son; today I have begotten you (Ps. 2:7). And the writer to the Hebrews opens his letter by proving Christ's superiority to angels with two quotations, and the second of them is this verse: to which of the angels did God ever say... "I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son"? (Heb. 1:5).

And then: when he commits iniquity, I will discipline him.

Which cannot be said of Christ. He committed no iniquity, and no one has ever suggested otherwise.

The honest thing is to hold both rather than collapse either, because the New Testament does exactly that. This promise has a near referent and a far one. Near, it is Solomon and the line of kings after him — sinners, disciplined, sometimes disastrously, and never removed. Far, it reaches past every one of them to a son of David whose throne actually is forever, and the New Testament writers reach back for it with complete confidence.

Gabriel quotes it to a girl in Nazareth: the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32-33). Peter preaches it at Pentecost: David knew that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne, and applies it to the resurrection (Acts 2:30). And the last chapter of the Bible has Jesus saying I am the root and the descendant of David (Rev. 22:16).

There is a strand of Old Testament prophecy that works like this all the way through. The sentence lands on a man standing in front of you and keeps travelling.

'"but my steadfast love will not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away from before you."'

This clause is why the whole thing is different in kind from anything before it.

My steadfast love is hesed again, and here it is God's. Will not depart from him.

Saul is named, and named as the contrast. Saul sinned and the kingdom was taken; the anointing was transferred; the Spirit departed; God would not answer him by dreams or Urim or prophets, and he died on a mountain having been told the day before. That is what removal looks like.

David's line will sin too — Solomon will go after other gods in his old age, and the kings after him will be a catalogue of idolatry and folly — and the discipline is promised in advance and it is not gentle. The rod of men, the stripes of the sons of men. David will feel the first stroke of it in chapter 12, in his own household, and it will run through the rest of his life.

But the love does not go.

That is the difference between a relationship with terms and a relationship with a promise underneath it. Discipline is what happens to sons. Removal is what happened to Saul. And any Christian who has ever wondered whether a particular failure has finally put them outside is standing in front of this verse, because the New Testament makes exactly this argument: the Lord disciplines the one he loves... it is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons (Heb. 12:6-7).

'"And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever."'

Three certainties and two forevers, and then it stops.

'In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.'

A short verse doing quiet work.

Nathan delivers the whole thing, including the part that reverses what he himself said the day before, and including the sentence that tells the king he will not be building anything. He does not soften it, delay it, or shape it into something easier to receive.

That is what a prophet is for, and it is why this man can be trusted five chapters later when he walks in with a story about a lamb.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–24 — Who Am I, O Lord GOD?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?" (v. 18). And it was a small thing in your eyes even to do that: you have spoken also of your servant's house for a great while to come, and this is instruction for mankind, O Lord GOD! (v. 19). Because of your promise, and according to your own heart, you have brought about all this greatness (v. 21). Therefore you are great, O LORD God. For there is none like you, and there is no God besides you (v. 22). And then Israel: who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: He sits. Israelites usually stood or knelt or lay flat to pray, and the posture here is neither petition nor protocol — it is a man who has been handed something too large to stand up under, sitting down in front of God with it.
verseByVerse.examples: The prayer never asks for anything until verse 25. Its whole first half is about who God is and what God has done, and when David finally moves off himself he moves not to his dynasty but to the nation: who is like your people Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far? And yet this was a small thing in your eyes, O Lord GOD. You have spoken also of your servant's house for a great while to come, and this is instruction for mankind, O Lord GOD! And what more can David say to you? For you know your servant, O Lord GOD! Because of your promise, and according to your own heart, you have brought about all this greatness, to make your servant know it. Therefore you are great, O Lord GOD. For there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears. And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making himself a name and doing for them great and awesome things by driving out before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, a nation and its gods? And you established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever. And you, O LORD, became their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?"'

He goes in and sits down.

The posture is unusual enough that commentators have been remarking on it for centuries. Israelites stood to pray, or knelt, or lay face down; Solomon knelt at the dedication of the temple, Ezra fell on his knees, Daniel knelt three times a day. Sitting is not the posture of petition and it is not the posture of ceremony.

It is what a man does when he has been handed something he cannot stand up under.

He has not come to ask for anything — he will not ask for a single thing until verse 25. He has come to be in the presence of what has just been said to him, and he sits down in front of the ark in the tent he pitched, and starts talking.

'"Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?"'

The question is not a formula and it is not modesty.

He has just been told his family will hold a throne forever, and the honest response to that from the eighth son of a Bethlehem farmer is who am I? He knows the answer. The last time anybody described him at length it was as a man with a sling standing in a valley, and before that as the one who was out with the sheep.

And what is my house — the same word again, third sense: not a palace and not a dynasty but simply his family, which is nobody in particular. Jesse's people were farmers in a small town, and Jesse's great-grandmother had walked in from Moab with nothing.

'"And yet this was a small thing in your eyes, O Lord GOD. You have spoken also of your servant's house for a great while to come, and this is instruction for mankind, O Lord GOD!"'

The last clause of that verse is one of the harder pieces of Hebrew in the book, and it is better to say so than to pretend.

The words are literally something like and this is the law of the man — torat ha'adam. Translators go different ways. Some read it as a statement: this is the charter, or the instruction, for humanity — meaning that what God has just promised David is his way of dealing with the whole human race, not merely one family's succession. Others read it as a question, as the older English versions did: is this the manner of man? — meaning, do human beings deal with each other like this? Both readings are defensible and the grammar does not decide between them.

What is not in doubt is the astonishment underneath, and the two readings are not far apart in effect. Either David is saying that this promise is about more than himself and reaches out to mankind, or he is saying that nobody has ever behaved like this. And in either case he has grasped that something has just happened which is out of proportion to the occasion.

'"And what more can David say to you? For you know your servant, O Lord GOD!"'

You know your servant.

He gives up trying to respond adequately, and the reason he gives is the best one available. There is no point telling God what this means to him, because God already knows — knows him better than he knows himself, which will be demonstrated with terrible thoroughness in five chapters.

'"Because of your promise, and according to your own heart, you have brought about all this greatness, to make your servant know it."'

Two reasons are given for everything that has happened, and neither one is David.

Because of your promise. And according to your own heart.

That second phrase is the deeper of the two. God did this because of what he is like. Not because of anything found in David and not because of any need in himself — the reason for the covenant is in God's own character, which is the only place any covenant in Scripture is ever grounded.

'"Therefore you are great, O LORD God. For there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears."'

The prayer turns into praise and the subject changes from what David has been given to who gave it.

Note the word therefore. He does not begin with God's greatness as a formality; he arrives at it, out of what has just been done to him. This is theology reasoned from experience.

'"And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making himself a name and doing for them great and awesome things by driving out before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, a nation and its gods?"'

Now watch where he goes, because it is not where anybody would expect.

He has just been promised an eternal throne for his own family. He turns to the exodus and to the nation.

Who is like your people Israel — the same construction he used of God one verse earlier, now used of Israel: there is none like you, and there is no nation like this one. And the reason is entirely about God's action. The one nation on earth whom God went to redeem. God went. He came down to Egypt and got them out.

Note also making himself a name. Two verses about names, and the same point in both: God gave David a great name in verse 9, and God made a name for himself in the exodus. Names are things God confers, including his own reputation, and the exodus was as much about who God is as about who Israel is.

'"And you established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever. And you, O LORD, became their God."'

The covenant formula, in its oldest form: you shall be my people and I will be your God.

The man with the newest and largest promise in Israel's history reaches back to the oldest one, and puts his own dynasty inside it. What he has been given is not a new arrangement running alongside what God did at Sinai. It is the same arrangement, going forward.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–29 — Do as You Have Spoken
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And now, O LORD God, confirm forever the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house, and do as you have spoken (v. 25) — so that your name will be magnified forever (v. 26). And the reason he dares to ask at all: for you, O LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have made this revelation to your servant, saying, "I will build you a house." Therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you (v. 27). And now, O Lord GOD, you are God, and your words are true, and you have promised this good thing to your servant (v. 28). Now therefore may it please you to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: He prays the promise back. Every request in this half of the prayer is a quotation of something God has just said, handed back with do as you have spoken attached — which is not informing God of anything but taking him at his word in his hearing.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 27 says where the courage came from, and it is not from David. You have made this revelation... therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer. He would never have dared ask for a dynasty. He asks because he was told first.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O LORD God, confirm forever the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house, and do as you have spoken. And your name will be magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts is God over Israel,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you. For you, O LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have made this revelation to your servant, saying, 'I will build you a house.' Therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you. And now, O Lord GOD, you are God, and your words are true, and you have promised this good thing to your servant. Now therefore may it please you to bless the house of your servant, so that it may continue forever before you. For you, O Lord GOD, have spoken, and with your blessing shall the house of your servant be blessed forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"And now, O LORD God, confirm forever the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house, and do as you have spoken."'

Here is the first request in the prayer, and it arrives seven verses in.

Do as you have spoken.

Read what he is actually doing, because it is the pattern of every great prayer in Scripture. He is not proposing anything. He is not telling God about a need. He takes the promise God has just made, and hands it back, and asks God to do it.

That is praying the promise. Abraham does it over Sodom, holding God to his own justice. Moses does it on the mountain after the golden calf, and the argument he uses is God's oath to Abraham (Ex. 32:13). Daniel does it with Jeremiah's seventy years open in front of him (Dan. 9:2). And the Lord Jesus taught his disciples to pray your kingdom come, which is asking God for the one thing he has already announced he will do.

There is nothing presumptuous in it, and there is nothing informative in it either. God is not being reminded. He is being taken at his word in his own hearing, which is the sincerest thing a person can do with a promise.

'"And your name will be magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts is God over Israel,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you."'

Look at the order he puts things in when he asks.

God's name first, and David's house second, and the second clause is the consequence of the first. He is not asking for the dynasty for its own sake. He is asking for it because a permanent house of David will be a permanent advertisement that the LORD of hosts is God over Israel.

Whether he could have kept that order under pressure is another question, and chapter 11 is the answer. But he has it right here, and it is the same order as 5:12.

'"For you, O LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have made this revelation to your servant, saying, 'I will build you a house.' Therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you."'

This verse tells us where the boldness came from, which is a question worth asking.

Therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer.

Literally, he found his heart. He would never have dared. Sitting down in front of God and asking him to establish your family on a throne forever is not a thing a man thinks up on his own — and the whole reason David can ask for it is that God said it first.

The promise is what makes the prayer possible. Take away verse 11 and verse 27 is presumption; with verse 11, it is obedience.

That is the answer to a question most Christians have felt at some point without putting it into words: what am I actually allowed to ask for? Here is one answer that will carry a great deal of weight. You may ask for what he has said he will do. The size of the request is not the issue; the warrant for it is.

'"And now, O Lord GOD, you are God, and your words are true, and you have promised this good thing to your servant."'

Three statements, and they are the ground of everything he has said.

You are God. Your words are true. You have promised this good thing. Take any one of those away and the prayer collapses. Together they are the whole basis of confidence: the one who spoke is God, what he says corresponds to reality, and this particular thing has actually been said.

'"Now therefore may it please you to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you. For you, O Lord GOD, have spoken, and with your blessing shall the house of your servant be blessed forever."'

He ends where the whole conversation began, on the word house, and by now it has travelled a long way.

He came in wanting to build one. He is going out having been given one, and asking that it may stand.

Now step back from the chapter, because it is the hinge of the Old Testament, and a great deal hangs on it.

Everything after this in Israel's story is read against this promise. The prophets appeal to it when the monarchy is collapsing — Isaiah's child who will sit on the throne of David and over his kingdom... from this time forth and forevermore (Isa. 9:7); Jeremiah's righteous Branch raised up for David when there is nothing left of the dynasty but a king in a Babylonian prison (Jer. 23:5).

And when the line runs out, the promise does not. There is a period of centuries with no son of David on any throne anywhere, and then an angel stands in front of a girl in a village and says the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David... and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32-33).

A thousand years between the promise and the birth. God had taken fifteen years to give David a crown and had explained nothing; here he takes a millennium, and the promise holds the whole way.

And the last thing to say about the chapter is the simplest. David wanted to build God a house and was told no. What he got instead was a son who would build the house, and a Son whose house would never fall, and the discovery every believer eventually makes: the thing you wanted to give God turns out to be the occasion on which he gives you something you would never have dared to ask for.

7.theology:
Nathan is wrong, and that is the point (vv. 3-5). He is not a flatterer or a fraud; he is the prophet who will confront a murderer to his face. Here he answers immediately with his own opinion — and look how good the opinion is: godly proposal, pure motive, the LORD's anointed at the height of his obedience in a season of obvious blessing. Every indicator points one way, and the conclusion is wrong. There is a difference between good counsel and the word of God, and the difference is not the godliness of the counsellor. The LORD is with you is not a guarantee that a particular plan is his. And Nathan comes back the next day and reverses himself in front of the king (v. 17), which is why he can be trusted five chapters later.

God never asked (vv. 6-7). The tabernacle was designed to be taken down and carried, because the people it belonged to were going somewhere and God intended to go with them. Othniel, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, Samuel — not one of them was ever told God wanted a building or reproached for not providing one. It is entirely possible to want something for God that God has not asked for, out of real love, and be wrong; the test of a plan is not how much devotion went into it.

Why David may not build. This chapter does not say, and readers ask. The reason comes later in David's own mouth: you have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name (1 Chron. 22:8; 28:3). The man who secured the land by war is not the man who builds the house of peace — and his son's name means peace.

Every verb belongs to God (vv. 8-11). I took you, I have been with you, I have cut off, I will make, I will appoint, I will plant, I will give you rest, the LORD will make you a house. David came offering to do something for God and received a recital in which God is the subject throughout. And a great name is not incidental: at Babel men said let us make a name for ourselves and were scattered (Gen. 11:4); to Abram God said I will make your name great and the covenant followed (Gen. 12:2). It is a thing men grasp at and God gives, and it never works the first way.

The people before the dynasty (v. 10). God speaks of Israel's security before he speaks of David's house, which is the same order as 5:12 and the same order David keeps in his own prayer at verse 26. The dynasty exists for the nation.

Two levels, and neither can be dropped (vv. 12-16). Near: Solomon, who does come from David's body and does build the house (1 Kings 8:20), and who is disciplined. Far: forever, three times in five verses, which is not the language of an ordinary succession. Verse 14 holds both in one sentence — I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son is quoted of Christ in Hebrews 1:5, and when he commits iniquity cannot be said of Christ at all. The honest thing is to hold both rather than collapse either, which is exactly what the New Testament does: Gabriel at Luke 1:32-33, Peter at Acts 2:30, and Jesus himself at Revelation 22:16. A strand of prophecy works like this throughout — the sentence lands on a man standing in front of you and keeps travelling.

As I took it from Saul (v. 15). Saul sinned and the kingdom went, the anointing transferred, the Spirit departed, and God stopped answering him by dreams or Urim or prophets. That is removal. David's line will sin too, and the discipline is promised in advance and is not gentle — the rod of men, the stripes of the sons of men, and the first stroke lands in chapter 12. But the hesed does not go. That is the difference between a relationship with terms and a relationship with a promise underneath it, and the New Testament argues from exactly this ground: the Lord disciplines the one he loves... God is treating you as sons (Heb. 12:6-7).

He sat down (v. 18). Israelites stood, knelt, or lay flat; Solomon knelt at the dedication, Daniel three times a day. Sitting is neither petition nor protocol. It is what a man does when he has been handed something he cannot stand up under — and he asks for nothing at all until verse 25.

The difficult clause (v. 19). Torat ha'adam is literally something like the law of the man, and translators divide. Read as a statement: this is the charter for humanity — what God has promised David is his way of dealing with the whole human race. Read as a question, with the older English versions: is this the manner of man? — do people deal with each other like this? The grammar does not decide, and both come to much the same astonishment.

Two reasons, and neither is David (v. 21). Because of your promise, and according to your own heart. The ground of the covenant is in God's character, which is the only place any covenant in Scripture is ever grounded. And when David finally moves off himself he moves not to his dynasty but to the exodus and the nation: who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem. God went.

Praying the promise back (vv. 25, 27). Do as you have spoken is not informing God of anything — it is taking him at his word in his hearing, and it is the pattern of every great prayer in Scripture: Abraham over Sodom, Moses on the mountain arguing from God's oath to Abraham (Ex. 32:13), Daniel with Jeremiah's seventy years open in front of him, and your kingdom come. And verse 27 says where the boldness came from: you have made this revelation... therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer. He would never have dared. Take away verse 11 and this is presumption; with verse 11 it is obedience — which answers a question most Christians have felt without stating: you may ask for what he has said he will do. The size of the request is not the issue; the warrant is.

What hangs on this chapter. Everything after it is read against it. Isaiah's child on David's throne from this time forth and forevermore (Isa. 9:7); Jeremiah's righteous Branch raised up when nothing is left of the dynasty but a king in a Babylonian prison (Jer. 23:5). Then centuries with no son of David on any throne anywhere — and an angel in a village. God took fifteen years to give David a crown and explained nothing; here he takes a thousand years, and the promise holds the whole way. David wanted to build God a house and was told no, and got a son who would build the house and a Son whose house would never fall.
7.examples:
Then: A king sat in a cedar palace, decided the tent God lived in was not good enough, and was told by God that he had never asked for a building in four hundred years — and then, in the same breath, that he intended to give this man's family a throne that would not end. And the king went in and sat down on the ground in front of a tent and asked for nothing for seven verses.

Now: Two things, and the first is uncomfortable because it concerns good advice. Nathan was a real prophet giving a godly answer about a godly plan, and it was still only his opinion. A proposal can be devout, strategically sound, blessed by every visible circumstance and endorsed by someone genuinely spiritual, and still not be what God has asked for — and the LORD is with you settles nothing about any particular plan. The second is verse 27. Most people pray timidly because they are not sure what they are entitled to ask for. David asked for a dynasty forever, and the reason he dared is that God had said it first. Find what he has actually promised, and then ask for that, and ask for it plainly: do as you have spoken.

8.title: David's Victories
8.text: <sup>1</sup>After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and David took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines.<sup>2</sup>And he defeated Moab and he measured them with a line, making them lie down on the ground. Two lines he measured to be put to death, and one full line to be spared. And the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.<sup>3</sup>David also defeated Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to restore his power at the river Euphrates.<sup>4</sup>And David took from him 1,700 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses but left enough for 100 chariots.<sup>5</sup>And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians.<sup>6</sup>Then David put garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.<sup>7</sup>And David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem.<sup>8</sup>And from Betah and from Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, King David took very much bronze.<sup>9</sup>When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer,<sup>10</sup>Toi sent his son Joram to King David, to ask about his health and to bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him, for Hadadezer had often been at war with Toi. And Joram brought with him articles of silver, of gold, and of bronze.<sup>11</sup>These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued,<sup>12</sup>from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and from the spoil of Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah.<sup>13</sup>And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt.<sup>14</sup>Then he put garrisons in Edom; throughout all Edom he put garrisons, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.<sup>15</sup>So David reigned over all Israel. And David administered justice and equity to all his people.<sup>16</sup>Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army, and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder,<sup>17</sup>and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests, and Seraiah was secretary,<sup>18</sup>and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and David's sons were priests.
8.overview:
A chapter of campaign summaries, moving fast because it is meant to. The last chapter was a man sitting on the ground in front of a tent being told his house would stand forever; this one is the same man doing his job for perhaps twenty years, compressed into eighteen verses. The two belong together: chapter 7 promised that God would cut off his enemies and give Israel a place to be disturbed no more, and this is the promise being kept in the ordinary currency of a reign.

Two things in the catalogue stop a reader. The Moab measurement is savage — prisoners made to lie in a row, a cord stretched along them, two lengths killed and one spared by where a man happened to be lying — and the text supplies no provocation, no divine command and no comment. A reader will remember that David sent his own parents to Moab for safety, and that Ruth the Moabitess was his great-grandmother. Manufacturing a reason the writer withheld is not a service to anybody. And the hamstrung horses are the opposite: he destroys the finest cavalry in the region on the day he captures it, because the law said Israel's king must not acquire many horses. Solomon will have forty thousand stalls.

Then the verb the chapter turns on: dedicated. The tribute of a friendly king and the plunder of six nations, all of it set apart for the LORD — and Chronicles says plainly that this is the treasure Solomon builds the temple with. A man told he may not build it spends twenty years paying for it and never sees a stone laid.

And one sentence covers the domestic government, which is the right one: David administered justice and equity to all his people. Keep it. Seven chapters from now Absalom will stand at the city gate every morning telling every man with a lawsuit that nobody has been appointed to hear him — and a rebellion will be built entirely on the claim that this verse has stopped being true.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The LORD Gave Victory to David Wherever He Went
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David defeats the Philistines and takes Metheg-ammah (v. 1). He defeats Moab, and measures the prisoners with a line — two lines he measured to be put to death, and one full line to be spared (v. 2). He defeats Hadadezer of Zobah, capturing chariots and horsemen and hamstringing all the chariot horses but leaving enough for a hundred chariots (vv. 3-4). Twenty-two thousand Syrians fall when Damascus comes to help, and garrisons are put in Aram (vv. 5-6). And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verseByVerse.theology: The Moab measurement is savage and the text supplies no reason for it whatever — no provocation named, no divine command cited, no comment offered. A reader will also remember that David sent his own father and mother to Moab for safety when he was a fugitive (1 Sam. 22:3-4), and that his great-grandmother was Ruth the Moabitess. The writer records and does not explain.
verseByVerse.examples: The hamstrung horses are the opposite: that is obedience. The law told Israel's king he must not acquire many horses for himself (Deut. 17:16), and David keeps enough for a hundred chariots and disables the rest. Solomon will have forty thousand stalls (1 Kings 4:26).

verseByVerse.quote: After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and David took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines. And he defeated Moab and he measured them with a line, making them lie down on the ground. Two lines he measured to be put to death, and one full line to be spared. And the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute. David also defeated Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to restore his power at the river Euphrates. And David took from him 1,700 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses but left enough for 100 chariots. And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians. Then David put garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went. And David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem. And from Betah and from Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, King David took very much bronze.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and David took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines.'

A chapter of campaign summaries, and it moves fast because it is meant to.

The previous chapter was the theological summit of the book — a man sitting on the ground in front of a tent being told his house would stand forever. This one is the same man doing his job for what is probably twenty years, compressed into eighteen verses.

The two belong together. The promise of chapter 7 said God would cut off all your enemies from before you and give Israel a place where they would be disturbed no more (7:9-10). Chapter 8 is that happening, and the writer is showing the promise being kept in the ordinary currency of a reign.

'And he defeated Moab and he measured them with a line, making them lie down on the ground. Two lines he measured to be put to death, and one full line to be spared. And the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.'

This is one of the ugliest verses in the book, and it will not be softened here.

Prisoners are made to lie down in a row on the ground. A measuring cord is stretched along them. Two cord-lengths of men are killed and one cord-length is allowed to live, and the selection is made by where a man happens to be lying.

The text offers no justification of any kind. There is no provocation described, no atrocity avenged, no command of God cited, and no comment from the narrator afterwards. He states what happened in one sentence and moves to the next campaign.

Two things a reader will feel, and both should be named rather than suppressed.

The first is the irony. When David was a fugitive with a price on his head, the country he sent his father and mother to for safety was Moab — please let my father and my mother stay with you, till I know what God will do for me (1 Sam. 22:3-4). And he had family reasons for choosing it: his great-grandmother was Ruth, who came out of Moab to Bethlehem and would not go back. There is Moabite blood in the man measuring the cord.

Some have supposed that the Moabites betrayed or killed his parents, and that this is the answer to it. It is possible. The text does not say so, and inventing a reason the writer withheld is not a service to anybody.

The second is what the silence means. This narrator does not comment on much. He did not comment when David killed villages to protect a lie at Ziklag, or when Joab murdered Abner, or when David took more wives after learning the kingdom was for the people's sake. He records. And a reader who has learned how he works knows by now that the absence of approval is not an absence of judgment.

The Chronicler leaves the whole episode out.

'David also defeated Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to restore his power at the river Euphrates.'

'And David took from him 1,700 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses but left enough for 100 chariots.'

Here, in the middle of the same campaign report, is an act of deliberate obedience that costs him a great deal.

He has just captured the finest cavalry force in the region. Chariot horses were the heavy armour of the ancient world — the thing Israel had never had and had been terrified of since the days of the judges. Any king in the region would have absorbed them into his own army immediately.

He hamstrings them. The tendon is cut, the animal can never pull a chariot again, and a fortune in military capability is deliberately destroyed on the field.

He keeps a hundred.

Why? Because of a sentence in the law about kings, in the same short passage that warned about wives: only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses (Deut. 17:16).

The reason given in the law is about trust. A chariot corps is the thing a nation leans on instead of God, and the psalms say so directly — some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps. 20:7), which is very likely David's own line.

So he obeys a command that costs him a strategic advantage, on the day he wins it.

Set that beside his son. Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen (1 Kings 4:26), and he imported them from Egypt, which is the second thing the law forbade in the same breath. The father cut the tendons; the son built the stables.

And it is the same law, three verses further on, that David is breaking in his own household by taking wives. Nobody obeys the whole of it.

'And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians. Then David put garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute.'

'And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.'

There is the sentence the chapter is built around, and it will come again in verse 14.

Everything between the two occurrences is enclosed by it. The tactics are real, the soldiering is real, the numbers are large and the men who fell were killed by other men. And the writer will not allow the account to be read as a list of David's achievements.

The LORD gave. It is the same verb as the answers David kept getting from the ephod: I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand. The king who asked before every battle is the king who is now being told, by the historian, whose the victories were.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — These Also King David Dedicated to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Toi of Hamath, whose own enemy has just been destroyed for him, sends his son with gifts of silver, gold and bronze (vv. 9-10). These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued — and the list runs Edom, Moab, Ammon, Philistia, Amalek, and the spoil of Hadadezer (vv. 11-12). Eighteen thousand Edomites fall in the Valley of Salt, and garrisons go into Edom (vv. 13-14). And the refrain again: and the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verseByVerse.theology: Everything goes to the LORD. Not a share, not a tithe of the spoil — the tribute of a friendly king and the plunder of six defeated nations, dedicated. A man who has just been told he may not build the temple spends the rest of his reign paying for it.
verseByVerse.examples: The Chronicler makes that explicit: this is the treasure Solomon builds with (1 Chron. 22:14; 29:2-5). David was refused the work and gave everything he had to the work anyway, and never saw a stone of it laid.

verseByVerse.quote: When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer, Toi sent his son Joram to King David, to ask about his health and to bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him, for Hadadezer had often been at war with Toi. And Joram brought with him articles of silver, of gold, and of bronze. These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued, from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and from the spoil of Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah. And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt. Then he put garrisons in Edom; throughout all Edom he put garrisons, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer, Toi sent his son Joram to King David to ask about his health and to bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him, for Hadadezer had often been at war with Toi.'

A king David has never met sends his son with congratulations, and the reason is entirely practical: David has just destroyed the man who had been fighting Toi for years.

Hamath is far to the north, up beyond Damascus. This is the sound of the whole region recalculating.

'And Joram brought with him articles of silver, of gold, and of bronze.'

'These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued,'

Now this is the theological centre of the chapter, and it is a single verb: dedicated.

Not banked. Not distributed to the troops. Not spent on the palace, which he had every right to do and which every other king in the region did as a matter of course. Set apart for the LORD.

It is not a proportion. Read the list.

'from Edom, Moab, and the Ammonites, from the Philistines, from Amalek, and from the spoil of Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah.'

Six sources. The tribute of a friendly king in the north, and the plunder of every nation he has defeated, and the whole treasury of a Syrian empire.

All of it dedicated.

Now put that next to what happened one chapter ago, because the two verses are inseparable.

David asked to build God a house and was told no. The reason, given elsewhere in his own words, was blood: you have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name (1 Chron. 22:8).

So he cannot build it. And here is what he does about that, for the next twenty years: he wins wars and gives every penny of the proceeds to the project he has been forbidden to work on.

The Chronicler is explicit that this is where the temple's funding came from. David tells Solomon what he has laid up — a hundred thousand talents of gold, a million talents of silver, and bronze and iron beyond weighing — and adds that he had provided it with great pains (1 Chron. 22:14). At the end of his life he addresses the assembly and says he is giving his own personal fortune to it as well, because of my devotion to the house of my God (1 Chron. 29:2-5).

He never saw a stone of it laid. The foundations went in after he was dead.

There is something in that worth carrying away by anybody who has been told no about the thing they most wanted to do for God. David was refused the work and did not sulk, did not lose interest, and did not decide that if he could not build it, it was not his concern. He funded it for two decades and handed his son a finished budget and a set of plans.

Wanting the work done matters more than being the one who does it, and that is a harder test than the refusal was.

'And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt.'

The name again — and it should be read against chapter 7, where God said I will make for you a great name (7:9).

'And he put garrisons in Edom; in all Edom he put garrisons, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.'

The refrain, the second time, closing the catalogue.

Edom deserves a note, because a promise made in a tent centuries earlier is being kept in it. Edom is Esau's country, and what was said to Rebekah before the twins were born was the older shall serve the younger (Gen. 25:23). Isaac said the same to Jacob. It takes about eight hundred years and a battle in the Valley of Salt, and here it is: all the Edomites became David's servants.

That is how this book keeps score. God says a thing, and then history does it, slowly, by ordinary means, long after everybody who heard the promise is dead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Justice and Equity to All His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So David reigned over all Israel. And David administered justice and equity to all his people (v. 15). Then the cabinet: Joab over the army; Jehoshaphat recorder; Zadok and Ahimelech priests; Seraiah secretary; Benaiah over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David's sons were priests (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: One sentence covers the domestic government and it is the right one. Not conquest, not wealth — justice and equity to all his people, which is what a shepherd-king is for. Keep it: seven chapters from now Absalom will stand at the city gate telling everyone who comes that there is no man designated by the king to hear you (15:2-4), and the rebellion is built on the claim that this verse has stopped being true.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause is a genuine difficulty, since David's sons were not Levites and could not be priests in the ordinary sense. Chronicles renders the same list chief officials in the service of the king (1 Chron. 18:17), which is probably the sense — and it is better to say the term is uncertain than to invent a certainty.

verseByVerse.quote: So David reigned over all Israel. And David administered justice and equity to all his people. Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army, and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder, and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests, and Seraiah was secretary, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and David's sons were priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So David reigned over all Israel. And David administered justice and equity to all his people.'

Eighteen verses of conquest, and one sentence about how he governed — and it is the right sentence.

The summary of the reign is not the size of the empire, the tribute, the garrisons from Damascus to the Valley of Salt, or the treasury. It is justice and equity to all his people.

The two words are the standard pair in the Old Testament for good government: mishpat, which is judgment given rightly in actual cases, and tsedaqah, which is righteousness — doing right by people, particularly people who cannot enforce their own claims. Together they are what a king exists for.

And to all his people. Not to the ones with standing. That phrase is the test, and it is the reason the courts of the ancient world were judged by how they treated widows and foreigners and the poor, because those were the litigants nobody had to be fair to.

This is the same principle as 5:12 — the kingdom exalted for the sake of his people Israel — now shown in operation. He is the shepherd the elders called him at Hebron, and this is what shepherding a nation looks like on an ordinary Tuesday: hearing cases.

Hold on to this verse, because it is going to be quoted back at him.

Seven chapters from now his son Absalom will get up early every morning and stand beside the road into the city gate, and stop every man coming in with a lawsuit, and say to him: see, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you — and then, oh that I were judge in the land! Then every man with a dispute or cause might come to me, and I would give him justice (15:2-4).

That is a rebellion built entirely on the claim that verse 15 has stopped being true. And it works: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

Whether the claim was fair is a question the text leaves open, and the honest answer is probably that a kingdom this size had outgrown one man hearing cases, and that David had not noticed. What is certain is that a son found the one place his father was no longer paying attention, and stood in it every morning for four years.

'Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder;'

Joab is still there.

Five chapters ago he murdered the commander of the opposing army inside a city of refuge and was cursed for it in public. Here he is at the head of the cabinet list, running the army, and he will still be running it thirty years from now when he kills the king's son against a direct order.

The writer does not remark on it. He simply puts the name at the top of the list, as he will again at 20:23, and lets the reader remember what David said: these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I (3:39).

'and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests, and Seraiah was secretary;'

Two priests, and the second name carries a history.

Ahimelech son of Abiathar — and Abiathar was the boy who escaped from Nob with the ephod in his hand when Doeg the Edomite killed eighty-five priests on Saul's order, and ran to David in the wilderness (1 Sam. 22:20-23). David said to him then: stay with me; do not be afraid... with me you shall be in safekeeping.

Two generations later his family is in the king's cabinet.

'and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and David's sons were priests.'

Benaiah is the head of the royal bodyguard, and the Cherethites and Pelethites are foreign troops — Cretan and Philistine mercenaries, most probably, men David came to know during his sixteen months at Ziklag. The king's personal guard is not Israelite, which is a shrewd arrangement in a country that has recently had a civil war.

Benaiah himself is one of the mighty men, and the writer will come back to him: he killed two Moabite champions, and a lion in a pit on a snowy day, and an Egyptian giant with the Egyptian's own spear (23:20-21). He ends up commanding Solomon's army after executing Joab.

The last clause is a puzzle and it should be admitted as one. David's sons were priests. They were not Levites, and the priesthood was closed to anyone outside Aaron's line. The word may be being used in a wider sense of royal officiants or advisers; the Chronicler, listing the same cabinet, writes that David's sons were the chief officials in the service of the king (1 Chron. 18:17), which is probably the meaning.

Saying the term is uncertain is better than inventing a certainty about it.

8.theology:
The refrain brackets everything (vv. 6, 14). And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went, twice, enclosing the whole catalogue. The tactics are real and the soldiering is real, and the writer will not let the account be read as a list of David's achievements. It is the same verb as the answers he kept getting from the ephod: I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand. The king who asked before every battle is now told by the historian whose the victories were.

Moab, and a silence that is not approval (v. 2). No provocation is named, no atrocity avenged, no command cited, and the narrator says nothing afterwards. This is the writer who also said nothing when David burned villages to protect a lie, when Joab murdered Abner, and when David took more wives immediately after learning the kingdom was for the people's sake. Anyone who has read him this far knows that the absence of approval is not an absence of judgment. Some suppose the Moabites had harmed the parents David entrusted to them; it is possible and the text does not say it, and the Chronicler omits the episode altogether.

He cut the tendons (v. 4). Chariot horses were the heavy armour of that world, the thing Israel had never had and had feared since the judges — and he destroys a fortune in captured capability on the field because of one clause: he must not acquire many horses for himself (Deut. 17:16). The reason the law gives is trust; a chariot corps is what a nation leans on instead of God, and the psalm says so, probably in David's own words: some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps. 20:7). His son built forty thousand stalls and imported them from Egypt, which is the other half of the same command. And three verses further on in that same law is the sentence David is breaking at home. Nobody obeys the whole of it.

Dedicated, and not a proportion (vv. 11-12). Not banked, not distributed to the troops, not spent on the palace — which every other king in the region did as a matter of course. Six sources, all of it set apart. And this is what he does with a refusal: forbidden to build the house because of the blood he has shed (1 Chron. 22:8), he funds it for twenty years, hands Solomon a finished budget and gives his own personal fortune on top (1 Chron. 22:14; 29:2-5), and dies before the foundations go in. Anybody told no about the thing they most wanted to do for God should sit with that: he did not sulk, lose interest, or decide it was no longer his concern. Wanting the work done matters more than being the one who does it, and it is a harder test than the refusal was.

Eight hundred years to a battle in a valley (v. 14). The older shall serve the younger was said to Rebekah before the twins were born (Gen. 25:23), and here it is: all the Edomites became David's servants. That is how this book keeps score — God says a thing, and history does it slowly, by ordinary means, long after everyone who heard the promise is dead.

Justice and equity to all his people (v. 15). The summary of the reign is not the empire or the tribute or the garrisons. Mishpat is judgment given rightly in actual cases; tsedaqah is doing right by people, especially those who cannot enforce their own claims. And all is the test — not the ones with standing, which is why the courts of that world were judged by their treatment of widows and foreigners and the poor. This is 5:12 in operation. And it is the exact ground Absalom will occupy: there is no man designated by the king to hear you... oh that I were judge in the land! (15:2-4), which stole the hearts of Israel. Whether the claim was fair the text leaves open; probably the kingdom had outgrown one man hearing cases and David had not noticed. What is certain is that a son found the one place his father had stopped paying attention and stood in it every morning for four years.

The names in the cabinet. Joab is still at the top of the list, five chapters after murdering a man in a city of refuge and being cursed in public, and he will still be there when he kills the king's son against a direct order. Ahimelech son of Abiathar is there too — and Abiathar was the boy who ran from the massacre at Nob with the ephod in his hand, to whom David said stay with me... with me you shall be in safekeeping (1 Sam. 22:23). Two generations later his family is in the cabinet. And David's sons were priests is a real difficulty, since they were not Levites; Chronicles renders the same list chief officials in the service of the king (1 Chron. 18:17), which is probably the sense. Better to say the term is uncertain than to invent a certainty.
8.examples:
Then: A king captured seventeen hundred horsemen and the best chariot force in the region, and then had almost every one of the horses hamstrung where it stood — destroying, deliberately, on the day he won it, the single military advantage every other kingdom around him was built on, because of one sentence in a book about what a king must not acquire.

Now: Two things. The dedicated spoil is the one to keep. David was told he could not build the temple, and his response was to spend the rest of his working life funding it, and he died before the first stone went down. Being refused the work you wanted is not the same as being released from caring whether it gets done, and the second test is much harder than the first — because the temptation after a no is to lose interest in the project altogether and call it acceptance. And verse 15 is the other: everything an authority is actually for is in that sentence, and the giveaway is the word all. Absalom's rebellion succeeded because a great many ordinary people had come to the city gate with a real complaint and found nobody listening.

9.title: Mephibosheth: Grace at the King's Table
9.text: <sup>7</sup>And David said to him, 'Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always.' <sup>13</sup>So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he always ate at the king's table. Now he was lame in both his feet. (ESV)
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is one of the most perfect pictures of grace in the entire Old Testament — a chapter so theologically shaped that it reads almost like a parable, though it is utterly historical. David, at the height of his power and peace, asks: Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake? The question is startling. In the ancient world, the surviving heirs of a previous dynasty were eliminated as a matter of political security; they were potential rallying points for rebellion, perpetual threats to the new king's legitimacy. David's question inverts this logic entirely: he is looking not for people to eliminate but for people to bless.
